fullText:
London — The involvement of a small American firm linked to associates of President Trump in an energy project in Bosnia and Herzegovina worth more than $1.5 billion has raised questions about how the White House could be using its leverage in the fragile Balkan state.

U.S. lawmakers accuse the Trump administration of lifting sanctions on Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik in an effort to enrich and empower allies of Mr. Trump, and of undermining longstanding U.S. foreign policy interests in the region in the process.

On Sunday, Mr. Trump was hailed by Dodik after his Serb nationalist party won one of Bosnia and Herzegovina's three presidency seats, which are split between Bosnia's Muslim minority, known as Bosniaks, as well as Serb and Croat ethnic groups under the country's complex power-sharing electoral system.

"If it had not been for Donald Trump's magnificent victory … we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told supporters in a speech, in which he also thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for his support.

AAFS Infrastructure & Energy, a company incorporated in the U.S. last year and headed by President Trump's former personal attorney Jesse Binnall and Joseph Flynn, the brother of Trump ally General Michael Flynn, is close to securing a contract to develop the Southern Interconnection Gas Pipeline.

The pipeline project has been discussed by Bosnian officials for years, but long opposed by Dodik, who has close ties with the Kremlin. But Dodik, whose party has veto power in Bosnia's parliament, said he would not stand in the way of the proposal following the announcement of AAFS' involvement last April. Six months earlier, the Trump administration lifted sanctions against Dodik that were imposed by the U.S. Treasury almost a decade ago.

The pipeline would connect Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia's gas network, allowing Bosnia to import liquefied natural gas (LNG) from its neighbors. The project, which is valued at around $1.7 billion according to the Croatian government, would help make Bosnia and Herzegovina less reliant on Russian gas imports.

On its website, AAFS describes itself as a company focused on "energy security, project structuring, capital alignment, and long-term regional infrastructure development."

The company does not appear to have demonstrable experience in any similar energy projects.

The secessionist leader Dodik, who until recently served as the president of Bosnia's self-governing, Serb-run territory called Republika Srpska, has long been accused of undermining the U.S. brokered Dayton Accords, which ended the bloody sectarian violence between Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia in the 1990s.

The sanctions, which included asset freezes and visa bans, were imposed by the Obama administration in 2017. The Biden administration then imposed further sanctions in 2022, accusing Dodik of corruption, including the charge that he had handed government contracts to close business associates in Republika Srpska.

A congressional report published last month by House Democrats, titled "Pay for Play in the Balkans," alleges that those two decisions — the removal of sanctions on Dodik and his decision to not oppose the pipeline — are directly linked.

"The Trump administration has used its diplomatic influence and connections with shady characters like Michael Flynn … to facilitate the concession contract for the SIC [Southern Interconnection Gas pipeline] to AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC, a company owned and operated by Michael Flynn's brother Joseph Flynn and Trump-affiliated lawyer and political activist Jesse Binnall," the report alleges.

AAFS Infrastructure and Energy LLC did not respond to a CBS News request for comment.

Foreign agent registration filings (FARA) cited in the report and reviewed by CBS News show that Michael Flynn, President Trump's former national security adviser, last worked as a paid lobbyist for Republika Srpska in October 2025, the month during which the sanctions against Dodik were lifted.

Those same filings show that Flynn was paid $100,000 for that work by RRB Strategies, a lobbying firm run by Rod Blagojevich, the former Illinois governor who was convicted in 2011 of 18 counts of corruption and spent nearly eight years in a federal prison before being pardoned by President Trump last year.

Flynn provided strategic advice and counsel, analysis and information research, and introductions to the Republika Srpska government, according to the FARA filings.

Blagoyevich's firm originally signed a contract to "provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska" in March 2025, separate FARA filings reviewed by CBS News show.

CBS News sought comment from email aliases associated with Flynn and Blagojevich, but did not receive any response by the time of publication.

On Nov. 13, 2025, the U.S. Embassy in Sarajevo said in a social media post that Chargé d'Affaires John Ginkel had met Bosnian Prime Minister Nermin Niksic to discuss the gas pipeline project and "to support the importation of U.S. gas through Croatia to consumers in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

One week later, the embassy announced a preliminary agreement for an "American company to develop, build, and manage the pipeline."

Four days after that, on Nov. 24, AAFS Infrastructure & Energy was incorporated in the state of Wyoming.

In January, the U.S Embassy in Sarajevo posted again confirming that a meeting had taken place between AAFS leadership, including Joseph Flynn and Binnall, and top Bosnian officials.

AAFS was then granted the status of lead investor and operator on the proposed natural gas pipeline in legislation passed by Bosnia's parliament in April.

Later that month, the Croatian and Bosnian governments signed a contract to construct the pipeline with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright in attendance for the signing ceremony. At a news conference with Bosnia's energy minister on April 2, Binnall hailed the pipeline project as a "priority" for the Trump administration.

The White House declined to comment on the pipeline project last week, but an administration official said the sanctions against Dodik were lifted to prevent instability in the Balkans.

"This is yet another example of President Trump's pragmatic, farseeing foreign policy that has prevented disasters on perennial issues that his predecessors so often stumbled into," a White House official told CBS News on Friday, without elaborating on the type of disasters the Trump administration was preventing.

A State Department letter published as part of the House Democrat-authored congressional report said the decision to delist Dodik had helped ensure peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The official who wrote the letter, Paul Guaglianone, said lifting sanctions against Dodik had led to Bosnian Serb separatists rolling back policies that would have destabilized Bosnia's government.

The lifting of sanctions "advanced U.S. interests in [Bosnia and Herzegovina] and the Western Balkans. On October 18, the Republika Srpska National Assembly (RSNA) withdrew most of the anti-Dayton legislation it had passed in recent years," the letter read. That legislation had included laws that would have blocked Bosnia's national police and judiciary from having any authority in Republika Srpska.

Political scientist and Balkans foreign policy expert Jasmin Mujanović told CBS News the legislation in question had already been struck down prior to the lifting of the sanctions against Dodik, and he was skeptical of the Trump administration's justifications for the move.

"This package of omnibus secessionist laws that the Serb nationalist authorities and the RS [Republika Srpska] entity in Bosnia had unlawfully voted through in the local assembly had already been struck down by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia Herzegovina," he said.

"If the argument is that the Trump administration nevertheless managed to get Dodik and his people to withdraw the laws, it's still unclear what the significance of that is, or for that matter, why, given that the laws are moot," he said, adding that it would "result in sanctions relief for an entire regime."

fullText:
‘Techno-optimism’ may lead to reliance on unproven solutions at expense of societal changes needed

Scientists who believe technology will largely solve the problems caused by the climate crisis are less likely to engage in civic action on the issue, according to a study.

The report from the London School of Economics found they are 23% less likelyto sign petitions or take part in protests than peers who doubt that technology is the answer. They are also 18% less likely to make high-impact lifestyle changes, from reducing flights to changing to a vegan or vegetarian diet.

Fabian Dablander, the lead author, said the belief that technology will largely solve climate change and its consequences, labelled “techno-optimism”, can lead to an over reliance on unproven solutions at the expense of the far-reaching socioeconomic transformations needed to address the climate and nature crisis.

“Technological solutions are often politically attractive because they promise to address climate change without requiring changes to how people live and consume,” said Dablander.

“Strikingly, we see the same tendency at the individual level, with greater faith in technological solutions going hand in hand with less engagement in climate action. Yet technology cannot substitute for the broader societal changes and large-scale shifts in consumption that are also needed.”

The study surveyed more than 9,000 scientists across 115 countries. Overall 27% said they agreed with the statement “technology will largely solve the problems caused by climate change” and 44% disagreed (29% neither agreed nor disagreed).

The “techno-optimist” scientists reported engaging in less civic actions and protests, signed fewer petitions and engaged in less advocacy. They were also less likely to reduce the number of flights they took, cut their car usage or follow a mostly vegan or vegetarian diet.

The report, published in Environmental Research Letters, also found that techno-optimism was most prevalent among scientists with right leaning political views and those working in applied and natural sciences.

Prof Kevin Anderson, one of the world’s leading climate scientists, of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at the University of Manchester, who was not involved in the study, said in his experience “a significant proportion of climate academics who enjoy very high incomes from their work, particularly when those incomes are accompanied by prestige, status and glittering honours, have enthusiastically swallowed the blue pill”.

“It offers a convenient escape from any uncomfortable sense of personal responsibility, allowing them to maintain the comforting fiction that they are deeply concerned about the world their children will inherit while continuing to live lives that contribute disproportionately to the problem.”

He added the “accompanying faith in future technological salvation provides another crutch: a way of postponing difficult choices today by placing hope in solutions that may arrive tomorrow”.

“Yet strikingly often, the evidential basis for these promises falls far short of the standards of scrutiny they would demand of research conducted by others. The result is a remarkable inversion of scientific practice: the more uncomfortable the implications of the evidence, the greater the enthusiasm for believing in a future that the evidence does not support.”

fullText:
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) dropped by almost 800,000 barrels last week, and the Trump administration moved forward with plans to sell another 40 million barrels in the coming months.

New data released on Monday by the US Department of Energy showed the US energy backstop sitting at 283 million barrels, down from 283.77 million the week prior.

That leaves about two weeks of US oil consumption in the reserve amid widespread worries about global stockpiles, which the head of Saudi Arabia's state producer on Monday called "scarily thin."

Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi Aramco, added at an Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday that releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but won't fix the imbalances that have developed between supply and demand.

Yet these withdrawals in the US could soon accelerate after the Trump administration unveiled a request for bids from companies to buy up to 40 million barrels of crude oil from the SPR, with the aim of having the companies return those supplies "with additional premium barrels." The solicitation process is ongoing, and it's unclear if companies will agree to those terms.

The Trump administration continues to wrestle with high energy prices, less than a month before the midterm elections, and is reportedly preparing an executive order to expand access ‌to tax-exempt diesel, with the president confirming on Monday afternoon, "I'll be helping [farmers] with diesel."

In recent days, G7 countries — including the US — announced a new set of plans to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency fuel, including "a frontloaded substantial diesel release."

A White House official told Yahoo Finance that Trump intends to follow through on a commitment to release a total of 172 million barrels from the SPR, which was announced earlier this year.

The US energy backstop already sits at the lowest level seen since October of 1982, and a withdrawal of another 40 million barrels would put the reserve at its lowest level since records began being kept earlier in 1982, as the backstop was still coming online under President Ronald Reagan.

For his part, President Trump continues to project confidence that the US reserves will be quickly refilled. He told a crowd in Alabama over the weekend that, because of an energy deal with Venezuela, "we're going to be filling up very shortly our strategic reserves for nothing."

Experts say that, despite Trump's promises, refilling the reserves will be a complex and far-from-free process that could take years.

fullText:
LONDON — A British Airways passenger jet flying from London to Chicago descended 28,000 feet in just seven minutes after declaring an emergency due to an unspecified “technical issue,” the airline said Monday.

The Boeing 777 took off at 12:15 p.m. local time (7:15 a.m. ET) but started descending just 30 minutes later while flying over Ireland, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

The plane turned around and spent around four hours zigzagging over the Bristol Channel, a waterway to the west of England, before landing back at London Heathrow Airport at 5 p.m. local time (noon ET).

“The aircraft landed safely after our highly-trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue,” British Airways said in an emailed statement. “Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”

Heathrow did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Passengers will likely be put up in hotels by the airline until another flight can be arranged, as stipulated by the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.

Britain’s National Air Traffic Service (NATS) came under scrutiny last month after two technical problems in the space of two weeks caused major delays at several U.K. airports and hundreds of flights were canceled.

NATS blamed software issues for the delays.

Britain’s Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation had been “deeply frustrating” for passengers.

With 84.5 million passengers last year, Heathrow ranked seventh in the table of the world’s busiest airports, according to data published by Airports Council International.

Travel from Heathrow was severely disrupted in March last year when a massive fire at an electricity substation caused a predawn power outage at the global transport hub.

The closure affected more than 1,300 flights and 200,000 passengers.

After investigating 600 items of evidence related to the substation, the National Energy System Operator ruled out suspicious activity in a report saying a preventable moisture fault caused the fire, leaving almost 70,000 homes without power.

title: London City gelling, Man City flying - takeaways from WSL start
description: After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.
fullText:
After five frantic weeks, the Women's Super League takes a two-week break, offering the perfect chance to take stock of a thrilling start to the season.

Here are five key takeaways from the opening weeks.

For the first time this decade, the established order of the WSL looks under threat.

London City Lionesses and Tottenham have been bullish about climbing the table, while Liverpool also sought to kick on this season.

After five games, London City look the most convincing, with Sunday's statement 6-1 win at Spurs a dazzling example of the talent and depth manager Eder Maestre has at his disposal.

Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas headlined some eye-catching summer signings and she scored twice against Tottenham.

But it was the manner in which the whole team dismantled their previously impressive opponents that was so spectacular, with fellow forwards Kadidiatou Diani and Danielle van de Donk also looking a class above.

"This kind of win can be a game-changer," Maestre said.

No doubt. It is the kind of display that can lead to talk of a title charge.

For Spurs, a humiliating home loss is a reality check after promising early results.

Liverpool acquitted themselves well in narrow losses away to both Manchester clubs but, with key attacking players such as Vivien Endemann missing against United, they lacked creativity.

That points to perhaps the biggest thing both Liverpool and Spurs lack in comparison with London City: squad depth.

Five wins from five with 16 goals scored, defending champions Manchester City have picked up where they left off.

Sunday's comeback victory over Arsenal made it City's best start to a season since opening the 2017-18 campaign with seven straight victories, cementing their status as the team to beat.

In so doing, City also likely ended the Gunners' title aspirations even this early on.

It helps when their best players are performing. Khadija Shaw's contract renewal in the summer was key and the striker has five league goals already. England winger Lauren Hemp is also in fine form, contributing four goals and two assists.

After some quietly shrewd additions in Beth Mead, Carlotta Wamser and Niamh Charles, City look well set once again.

Their closest rivals are Chelsea, who have responded to an opening-day draw against Aston Villa by winning four straight games without conceding a goal.

While boss Sonia Bompastor wants them to be more clinical, their defensive strength is something they have over City.

As for Arsenal, the gap is 10 points to leaders City, and strong pre-season hopes of a first league title since 2018-19 are vanishing, with manager Renee Slegers conceding on Sunday: "At the moment, we are not in the conversation."

Manchester United's summer of upheaval bled into the start of the season, with Eva Olid's arrival from Hearts beginning with convincing defeats by London City and Chelsea.

The message from the club was that this would be a season of transition but recent performances suggest they are getting to grips with her style of play.

Saturday's 1-0 win over Liverpool was United's fourth straight victory in all competitions, with 18 goals scored in the process.

"I am so happy for the players - they deserve it," Olid said. "We have started to click in a lot of things and they fight for each other.

"But there is still a lot to improve. We created chances, but our last pass and our finishing needs to be better."

Summer signing Andrea Medina has been a huge positive on the left wing, with her contribution to the team more pronounced than a single goal suggests.

A trip to bottom side Charlton after the break is a presentable chance for more points before a stern test against Manchester City the following weekend.

This season is the WSL's biggest ever, literally, with the league expanding from 12 to 14 teams and three coming up from WSL 2.

Crystal Palace look the most comfortable of the promoted sides, boasting six points from five games and they moved to eighth in the WSL table by drawing at Aston Villa on Sunday.

But things are more difficult for the other promoted sides, Birmingham and Charlton, who prop up the table.

Despite some promising patches, WSL 2 champions Birmingham have just two points and one of those came against Crystal Palace.

At least France forward Oceane Hurtre looks suited to this level, sitting as joint top scorer in the WSL with five goals from five games.

Hurtre scored against Everton in defeat on Sunday but defender Neve Herron summed things up by saying Blues were "second to everything" after the game.

Meanwhile, it looks bleak for Charlton, bottom of the table with zero points, 15 goals against and only two goals scored.

After their 5-1 loss to Brighton on Sunday, goalkeeper and captain Sophie Whitehouse said: "It just wasn't good enough.

"It's a tough league. The jump up is so big. You can't make any mistakes."

Finally, it is too soon to draw conclusions but attendances at some of the league's biggest matches have been down on previous seasons.

For instance, Chelsea hosted Arsenal on 27 September in a fervent atmosphere, but the game had 36% fewer in Stamford Bridge than in January this year.

Similarly, Liverpool against Everton at Anfield was 19% down on last season, albeit the Merseyside derby was the first game of the 2025-26 season.

Three Saturdays ago, Arsenal kicked off against Manchester United at 17:30 in front of 29,853 fans. Last season, it was a lunchtime fixture that welcomed 37,627.

For balance, it ought to be highlighted that the Manchester City v Arsenal game on Sunday was promoted from the Joie Stadium to Etihad Stadium, and definitely had more than the 4,300 who attended the game last season.

Official figures have yet to be released for it.

Nevertheless, while this is a small sample size, paying customers is a potential trend to monitor as the WSL wrestles with the continued challenge of the schedule.

title: 'Money-grab' or celebration? NFL kicks off London series
description: The NFL kicked off this season's series of London games on Sunday but the build-up was overshadowed by anger from long-term fans over ticket prices.
fullText:
Once upon a time, tickets for NFL games in London were like gold dust.

All 43 games have been near capacity at Wembley, Twickenham and Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

According to the NFL, its UK fanbase has swelled to 18.6 million, with 4.5 million of those considered 'avid' fans.

So in the build-up to this year's London series, why were thousands of tickets still available for two of the three games?

Next week's clash between the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham sold out in hours.

But the crowd for Sunday's game at Tottenham between Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts only reached 60,907 after ticket prices were slashed, and large sections remain unsold for the Wembley game on 18 October.

The NFL is playing a record nine regular-season games abroad this season but 19 years after the first London game, has the NFL reached a saturation point in the UK?

Tickets to see Indianapolis beat Washington 30-13 on Sunday went on sale in July at £79-£245.

But the NFL then dropped prices twice, in late August and again last week. That meant some fans who paid £185 were sat next to fans who paid £79 a few days ago.

Some tickets were also discounted or free via the Blue Light Card and Tickets For Good platforms.

Matt Cullen has travelled from Cambridge to most of the London games and said there were two main reasons for the slow sales; a price hike and a season-ticket package being scrapped.

"I find the prices now mind-boggling," he added. "It's so far above the rate of inflation that it just feels like a money-grab. It's priced out a lot of long-term fans."

In 2019, tickets ranged from £55 to £125. According to Ticket-Compare,, external UK inflation has since risen by about 32.4% and the cheapest NFL London tickets have risen by 43.9%. The most expensive have seen a 96.5% hike.

Season-ticket packages had been available, guaranteeing seats for each London game with a discount, but they were scrapped after the 2024 season.

"It felt like a kick to the head for a lot of loyal fans who'd supported the games for a long time and spent a lot of money," said Cullen, a former season-ticket holder. "But I do understand the NFL wants to bring new fans in."

UK fans have also complained about the quality of recent match-ups in London when compared to those in the new countries where the NFL has expanded.

Australia hosted a divisional clash between the San Francisco 49ers and Los Angeles Rams last month, while the Baltimore Ravens and Dallas Cowboys played out a thriller in Brazil last week.

"It was an amazing game and we haven't had many of those unfortunately," added Cullen.

The best team coming to London this year is Philadelphia, who have reached two of the past four Super Bowls, and their game next week is a sell-out even though it was the most expensive.

The Jaguars face the Houston Texans in two weeks and Dave, another former season-ticket holder, will travel from Chorley.

"We were all gutted when they took the season tickets away," he admitted. "The way we saw it, we weren't wanted anymore because we didn't spend the money that new fans do on merchandise and we get to the stadium later.

"But it has opened it up for more fans to have the opportunity to attend so it's a double-edged sword."

BBC Sport spoke to dozens of fans at Sunday's game and none of them were aware ticket prices had dropped. None seemed to care either.

American fans know the London games don't provide the same tailgating experience they get back home, but they - and the players - are still fascinated by the eclectic crowd at international games.

Fans still travel from all over the UK, Europe and the US, wearing jerseys of all the NFL teams.

"It's still one of the greatest sporting events that neutrals can go to," said Dave. "I don't think there's any other sport where you'd get tens of thousands watching teams they don't support.

"It was always a celebration of the game. People would go for the love of the sport rather than the two teams that were playing and I think that's still the same."

It sure felt like a Washington home game when they recovered a Colts fumble on just the game's second play.

The crowd produced an even bigger roar when third-choice quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis - replacing the injured Marcus Mariota - made a 47-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks in the third quarter.

The Commanders thought they had drawn level when Antonio Williams ran in an 87-yard score, but the touchdown was chalked off for a Washington penalty.

Indianapolis quarterback Daniel Jones then got in to seal their success, with Jonathan Taylor having run in two touchdowns for the Colts.

It is hard to imagine anyone went home disappointed, no matter what price they paid.

The stands were bathed in sunshine and fans looked like they were having the time of their life as they sang Sweet Caroline and Wonderwall in unison.

Oasis' Noel Gallagher was booed when he appeared on the big screen - no doubt because of his football allegiance to Manchester City - and former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney was also among the crowd, wearing a half-and-half scarf.

Olympian Simone Biles travelled to London to support her husband Jonathan Owens, who is a safety for the Colts, and as long as stars such as those show up at NFL games, international fans will want to be there too.

"There's been a lot of anger from fans on social media about the ticket prices but it's only what they do with last-minute holidays," added Dave.

"Even though some of us fans see it as poor way for the NFL to run it, they've got a full stadium.

"We're just not used to dynamic pricing in the UK. It was the same with Oasis tickets for their reunion. We were outraged at that but we still all went didn't we."

title: London City Lionesses hit six past sorry Tottenham
description: Alexia Putellas and Kadidiatou Diani both score twice as London City Lionesses win in a rout against Tottenham, ending Spurs' unbeaten start in the Women's Super League.
fullText:
Tottenham Hotspur 1 - 6 London City Lionesses FT

Alexia Putellas and Kadidiatou Diani both scored twice as London City Lionesses hit six goals past Tottenham to end Spurs' unbeaten start to the Women's Super League campaign.

Putellas, a two-time Women's Ballon d'Or winner and a four-time Women's Champions League winner with Barcelona, grabbed her first WSL double following her summer move from Spain.

She had registered her first WSL goal in last week's 2-0 win over Brighton and only needed three minutes to open the scoring on Sunday at the BetWright Stadium.

The early strike came after Grace Geyoro's strike had been parried by home goalkeeper Lize Kop, with Putellas firing in the rebound with her left foot.

French forward Diani grabbed her first WSL goal in the 22nd minute when she got on the end of a fine move involving Freya Godfrey and Lucia Corrales.

Putellas scored her second and London City's third in the 34th minute with a shot into the roof of the net after Danielle van de Donk did superbly to get to the byeline to the left of goal and pull the ball back.

Tottenham nearly pulled a goal back just before the break through Julie Blakstad's well-struck free-kick, a left-footed attempt from 25 yards, but goalkeeper Elene Lete made an excellent save by pushing the ball on to the crossbar.

Van de Donk deservedly got a goal in the 52nd minute to make it 4-0, converting Diani's low cross from the right at the near post.

Tottenham immediately got one back as Victoria Pelova, a summer signing from Arsenal, scored for the fifth time in the WSL this season, controlling from Blakstad's cross and finishing well.

But London City restored their four-goal advantage when Kop's clearance was charged down by Diani, who had the easy task of walking the ball into an unguarded net.

London City grabbed a sixth in injury time when substitute Delphine Cascarino netted a fine individual goal, running at the home defence and performing a stepover to make space for the shot before firing past Kop.

Tottenham began the season with three wins and a draw from their opening four league matches.

A win on Sunday would have taken them top of the WSL, although that may have only been for a couple of hours with Manchester City, who won their opening four games, playing Arsenal later on.

But London City, given the huge investment they have made in their squad, look the more likely of these two to mount a title challenge.

They finished sixth in 2025-26 but made major signings in the summer, including Putellas and defender Mapi Leon from Barcelona, along with Diani from Lyon.

This was a fourth win in five WSL games, and its manner sends out a message.

Head coach Eder Maestre felt the result and performance would demonstrate to the rest of the league that his Lionesses can make a push for the title.

"The three points are the same as you can have in every game, but this kind of win can be a game changer in terms of showing everyone that we are pushing hard," said Maestre.

"But, at the same time, we need to be humble as well. The teams that are used to being there and occupying these places [at the top] are still there.

"I'm so happy we're hitting our targets. When you have these kind of players it is about trying to find chemistry and it takes time. It's a process and we're in the process of building something strong."

London City will not be in action for another two weeks because of the international break, and will hope that does not affect their momentum.

For Tottenham, the heavy defeat was a reality check.

Head coach Martin Ho said his team "looked scared with the ball" and added: "Really poor, not acceptable from us as a group. Defensively we didn't win a first ball, a second ball. Duels, we were poor. We have to move on.

"The team collectively needs to own that and we will, and that starts with me, I take responsibility for it.

"We were just not at it, but that can't be the level. Everyone will be disappointed - that was not the level we expect. We conceded six goals and you don't want to be doing that."

title: Jayden Daniels injury update: Latest on Commanders QB's status for today's game
description: Jayden Daniels is working his way back from a dislocated elbow. Will he play for the Commanders in Week 4 against the Colts in London?
fullText:
Jayden Daniels' season seemed in jeopardy. Until it wasn't.

The Washington Commanders quarterback dislocated his elbow for a second straight season in the team's Week 2 loss to the Dallas Cowboys. Things looked bleak in the immediate aftermath, with surgery being on the table for one of the league's young stars.

After an injury-riddled second season, that was the last thing that the 25-year-old needed. Yet surgery is on the back burner for now, and the elbow brace has come to the front, in hopes of saving the season for Daniels and the Commanders.

With the team set to kick off the London slate of games this season in Week 4, everyone wants to know: will Jayden Daniels be suited up for the international contest?

Daniels will not play in Week 4.

The Commanders signal-caller traveled with the team to London and returned to practice in a limited capacity ahead of Week 4. It represented a positive turn of events for Daniels, who failed to participate ahead of Week 3.

Daniels told reporters on Thursday, Oct. 1 that he was just taking everything "day by day" and wasn't surprised to be back on the field so quickly.

While he doesn't have a full range of motion with the brace on, Daniels vowed that it won't change anything about his game.

Overall, his concern level about reinjuring the elbow is low.

"That's what the brace is for," Daniels said. "If I had that concern, I would have gotten surgery."

The 25-year-old explained that he chose to avoid surgery for now because he wants to keep playing.

"I love playing football, I get paid to play football," Daniels said. "Everybody is hurting. I just feel for me being a leader, go out there and give it my shot to go out and play and obviously protect myself. I just love football and have a passion for it."

More: Will Jayden Daniels need elbow surgery? Experts explain 'unusual' reinjury

Daniels suffered a left elbow dislocation in Week 2.

X-rays showed no fracture, which was a good sign for Daniels' availability going forward. While he might eventually need surgery, there seems to be a chance that he could avoid it during the season by playing with a brace on.

Of course, it's unclear how the quarterback's elbow will react outside of a controlled practice setting.

The Commanders' performance without him and Daniels' ability to take hits could go a long way in determining his future availability.

Daniels appears to be on the fast track to return relatively soon.

His return to practice suggests he could return as early as Week 5 against the New York Giants. If Washington wants to err on the side of caution, the team has just two games left before a Week 7 bye after returning home from London.

While the Commanders would probably love to live in a world where Daniels doesn't get hurt, it's comforting to have a veteran like Mariota available to step in when needed. He is a steadying force with plenty of experience, and the Commanders have been able to lean on him.

title: London transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express?
description: With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question
fullText:
With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question

If Heathrow finally builds its third runway, Londoners can expect hundreds more planes flying overhead each day. But greater congestion on the ground will be a problem too. Under Heathrow’s £33bn expansion plan, 100,000-200,000 more passengers would eventually be travelling to or from the airport each day.

The most eye-catching problem has been moving part of the UK’s busiest motorway, the M25, to make space for a new 2.2-mile (3.5km) runway. A thornier one may be getting motorists out of their cars, and finding more sustainable ways for the extra passengers – and thousands of staff – to travel to and from Heathrow.

Although ride-sharing, coaches and buses can play a part, scaling up rail is the clear alternative. Space on the existing line is, however, at a premium, and the Elizabeth line, built with a promise of connecting business travellers swiftly and directly from Heathrow to the City and Canary Wharf, only has limited paths. With everything up for negotiation, transport experts are asking: has the time come to kill off the Heathrow Express?

The obvious airport train, as unwary visitors often find out too late, may not be the best one. The Heathrow Express, which charges a whopping £26 for a 15- to 21-minute one-way hop, was long one of the most expensive airport connections around (at least until it was overtaken by the Luton Dart). It is, as advertised, technically the fastest way to central London, though passengers travelling beyond Paddington may reach their destination more quickly on the Elizabeth line or even the tube on a direct route.

For those who value the speed – in addition to TV news, a toilet and a luggage rack – it may be the perfect service. But the Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers, with the number bolstered by airport staff on heavily discounted tickets.

Transport for London (TfL) has signalled its belief that the service’s time is up, as the government consults on its Heathrow expansion national policy statement. MPs must approve the statement for the runway to go ahead. That no longer seems automatic: Andy Burnham’s long-term scepticism over a third runway, along with the loss of Rachel Reeves in No 11 as a champion of expansion, makes Downing Street support look ambivalent at best – even given the new chancellor’s belated assertion that the “economic case stacks up”.

The Sunday Times reported this weekend that airport bosses have told ministers the third runway will not now be operational until 2039, a four year delay.

However many runways the airport has, TfL said it was “worth reviewing [the Heathrow Express’s] future in the context of determining the optimal mix of services on the Great Western mainline to make the most effective use of the limited capacity available”.

For TfL, the Elizabeth line, going deeper and cheaper into the heart of London, is “a more compelling service”. At the moment, only two Elizabeth line trains an hour serve Heathrow’s Terminal 5, which handles about 40% of the airport’s passengers. That means a passenger who does not carefully judge the timing may face a journey from the City or Canary Wharf to T5 of more than an hour. The frequency is due to double next year but more space into Heathrow could still be freed up.

Alex Williams, the chief customer and strategy officer at TfL, told MPs at a select committee hearing this month that the Heathrow Express was “taking up valuable paths that aren’t actually well used. There’s a way of repurposing that to be more affordable, more attractive, and carry more public transport users.”

Surface access, or getting people between central London and Britain’s biggest airport, underwent a step change with the Elizabeth line. Previously, the little-advertised offering Heathrow Connect joined the dots at the likes of Hayes & Harlington on a slower train to Paddington, serving many airport workers, if not international travellers. Fares were then about a third of the price of the Heathrow Express – a gap that is now less significant given that the Elizabeth line charges £15.50 to reach any of its central London stations. And for those who are able to book and plan a month ahead, the Express advance tickets can prove less expensive at £10.

TfL’s cheaper but slower alternative, the Piccadilly line (£5.90 into central London), is also due to get an upgrade of signalling and trains, increasing capacity.

Two additional rail schemes have been mooted – Heathrow Southern Railway and a Western Rail link – as ways to connect into the wider national rail network, and the Elizabeth line itself could be extended to Staines – all of which would encourage many more from the suburban commuter belt to take the train rather than drive to the airport.

Rebooting the railway now would coincide with the end of Heathrow Express’s operating agreement with the Department for Transport, which gives the service access rights to the national railway until June 2028. The DfT says no decision has yet been made on the future operation.

It’s complicated: the actual operator, the FirstGroup-owned Great Western Railway, is due to be nationalised this December and become part of Great British Railways next year. Meanwhile, Heathrow owns the stations and five miles of railway from the airport to the mainline, part of its original £1bn investment in the Express in the 1990s.

The service brought in revenue of £48m for the first six months of 2026, according to a Heathrow spokesperson. They said: “It operates without taxpayer funding and helps keep airport charges down. Passengers don’t want fewer choices – Heathrow Express remains an important part of the competitive connectivity, convenience and flexibility they expect.”

But many question whether enough is being done – or if there will be enough pressure on Heathrow to avoid gridlock on the roads. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, warned that the taxpayer could be left picking up the bill for public transport improvements “left undefined and unfunded in the current proposals” for expansion – estimated at up to £9bn by TfL, a figure Heathrow said it did not recognise.

Most passengers go to the airport by car. And while Heathrow is funding new car parks – with plans to boost its parking space capacity from 21,000 to 36,000 – and its rerouting of the M25, it has not pledged any of its £33bn expenditure on improving the trains, Williams told the select committee, adding: “If you make it easier for people to park very near the terminal, how will you encourage them to get on the train?”

Without clear demands for a mode shift to public transport – as existed in the previous expansion plan, as well as in the planning permission for Gatwick’s recently approved second runway – the policy statement was “a step backwards”, Williams said, adding that in 2017 “there was a commitment or an aspiration from Heathrow to get no extra traffic. That is gone.”

A DfT spokesperson said: “We are carefully considering responses to the consultation, which sets out the key requirements any future planning application for expansion would have to meet, including public transport targets.”

A legal mandate could happen, a source said. But so far these are just targets: at the most stringent, 55% of airport passengers using public transport, and only when Heathrow’s third runway is fully operational.

For Anthony Smith, the former passenger watchdog who now chairs the Heathrow Area Transport Forum, it seems a curious timetable. He told MPs: “If you’re trying to shift people out of cars in 20 years’ time, when you’ve got 130 million passengers, it’s just harder, harder, harder.”

title: Respect and laughs as Fury and Joshua face off
description: After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchange pleasantries, trade jokes and even discuss going for a pint at a news conference in London.
fullText:
After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.

The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come.

"He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."

On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.

There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event.

"It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said.

"I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."

The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.

Relive Fury & Joshua's jovial news conference

Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease

There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.

Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.

They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.

Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.

Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.

For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.

Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.

For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.

There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous.

"This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said.

"When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."

Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."

The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.

For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion.

"You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied.

"I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."

That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.

Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.

But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.

Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.

Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua.

"I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet."

"I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.

The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place at next year's unique two-day London Marathon.

Men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe was beaten by women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest.

As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's events taking place the following day on the traditional Sunday.

Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race.

"Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part."

Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event.

The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year.

In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than £150m will be raised for charitable causes.

The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.

"Our outstanding elite women's wheelchair field will begin the action just ahead of them, creating a true celebration of women's marathon racing," Brasher added.

The main events on both days will be a mixed field of male, female and non-binary participants.

title: Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease
description: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua arrive in London for Wednesday’s launch news conference, with their December fight now expected to take place as scheduled.
fullText:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua have both arrived in London before Wednesday's launch news conference for their fight.

It appears the all-British heavyweight contest - more than a decade in the making - remains on for 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium following several days of uncertainty.

Fury, 38, has travelled back from the United States, where he had been at Walt Disney World Resort with his family, while Joshua, 36, has flown in from his training camp in Dubai.

Fury-Joshua was officially announced on Thursday by Saudi powerbroker Turki Alalshikh, but doubts emerged 24 hours later amid a dispute over the role of UFC chief Dana White in the promotion.

Broadcaster Netflix said Alalshikh's The Ring and White would collaborate to promote the event, but Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.

White said on Saturday night he did not know whether the fight - or Wednesday's news conference - would happen. BBC Sport now understands he will not attend the launch.

A further potential hurdle emerged late on Monday over Fury's enrolment in the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (Vada) testing programme.

Fury's manager Spencer Brown has since said Fury is now enrolled with Vada, appearing to resolve another issue before the launch.

Fury and Joshua have never fought despite several previous attempts to make the all-British contest.

Wednesday's event at the British Airways ARC in Olympia will be the first time the pair have come face-to-face since the fight was officially announced, with a limited number of tickets also being made available to the public.

There was at least something reassuring about seeing both men step out of cars in London on Tuesday, ready for Wednesday's launch.

But a Fury-Joshua fight being 'on' has now been announced so many times it is hard to keep count.

And that is part of the problem. We have been here before and there is no way to dress up the past few days as anything other than a desperately poor look for boxing.

The majority of supporters felt Fury-Joshua had arrived too late, with both men now former champions and far from the peak of their powers.

Yet within 48 hours of the long-awaited announcement, even some of those still excited by the contest had been turned into cynics.

Instead of discussing how Fury and Joshua match up, the conversation became about promoters, contractual clauses, competing egos and whether the fight would happen at all.

That is remarkable for a shared purse reported to be worth close to $200m (£151m), backed by some of the most powerful figures in the sport.

Hearn has alleged contractual terms around White's involvement have not been adhered to. White has publicly attacked Hearn. Fury accused Joshua's camp of trying to pull out.

All of it created unnecessary uncertainty around a fight boxing has spent years failing to deliver.

With all that said, Wednesday offers an opportunity to change the mood quickly.

If Fury and Joshua both walk on stage and produce the kind of fireworks their rivalry had long-promised, some - though not all - of the noise of the past few days could fade.

title: Fury vs Joshua: December Superfight Faces Fresh Trouble Before London Press Conference
description: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are due to meet in London on Wednesday as the build-up to their long-awaited heavyweight […]
fullText:
Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are due to meet in London on Wednesday as the build-up to their long-awaited heavyweight fight takes another tense turn. Fury vs Joshua is set for December 11 at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, but fresh disputes over promotion and anti-doping testing have raised questions about the event in recent days.

The fight has taken years to arrange, with venue talks, contract issues and promotional disagreements repeatedly delaying it. Saudi boxing figure Turki Alalshikh confirmed the Cardiff date last week after Joshua's team pushed for the fight to remain in the United Kingdom. Fury and Joshua will now appear together for the first time since the fight was formally confirmed, with the event expected to draw global attention.

The Fury vs Joshua fight is scheduled for December 11 at Principality Stadium in Cardiff. The fight will stream globally on Netflix and is expected to begin in the early hours of December 12 in the United Kingdom to suit North American viewers.

Alalshikh confirmed the venue after months of discussions. Joshua's camp had pushed for a UK venue because of a clause in his contract. Promoters had previously considered Madison Square Garden and other U.S. locations.

The Fury vs Joshua fight will also feature the vacant WBA "super" heavyweight title, which Oleksandr Usyk vacated.

The Fury vs Joshua promotion faced another problem after Netflix and Ring Magazine materials listed Dana White as a co-promoter alongside Alalshikh's operation. Eddie Hearn, Joshua's long-time promoter, objected and said White's involvement conflicted with Joshua's agreement.

Hearn told Sky Sports there would be no press conference without his side being involved and said White would not attend.

Fury then questioned whether Joshua wanted the fight. He initially put the chances of the Fury vs Joshua bout happening at "one per cent" but later acknowledged that contracts had been signed and payments made.

"I do think it'll happen," Fury said. "Not unless they want to give the dough back."

Fury also said he expected to stop Joshua inside six or seven rounds and called him a "stepping stone" toward another fight with Usyk.

The Fury vs Joshua build-up also faced an anti-doping dispute. Joshua's team said both fighters were expected to enter the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association testing pool after signing their contracts.

Reports on Monday said Fury had not yet enrolled, creating uncertainty over whether Joshua would attend the London event. By Tuesday, reports from Ring Magazine's Mike Coppinger and Sky Sports indicated both fighters were traveling to London and the outstanding issues had been resolved enough for the press conference to go ahead. White is not expected to attend.

Fury and Joshua have known each other since sparring at Finchley Amateur Boxing Club in 2010. Their professional fight has since faced repeated delays over money, venues and promotional arrangements.

Fury, 38, returned from retirement earlier this year and stopped Mariusz Wach in July. Joshua, 36, stopped Jake Paul in December 2025 and then knocked out Kristian Prenga in July.

Together, Fury and Joshua have 66 wins, 52 knockouts and several world title reigns. Neither currently holds a major heavyweight belt. The December Fury vs Joshua fight remains one of boxing's biggest scheduled events, and Wednesday's London press conference will provide the next major update.

title: 5 arrested near air base used by U.S. in Iran war on suspicion of terrorism
description:
— U.K. police said Sunday that five men arrested in the middle of the night near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
London’s Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12:45 a.m.
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — U.K. police said Sunday that five men arrested in the middle of the night near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.

London's Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12:45 a.m. related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that is operated by the U.S. under an agreement dating back to the Cold War.

Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iranian missile sites under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28.

Iran has previously indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target.

Authorities are investigating a link between the Fairford arrests and Iran as one possibility.

The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of committing offenses under the Explosives Act in the Whelford area, which backs onto RAF Fairford that hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and the 420th Air Base Squadron.

Aerial footage from Sky News appeared to show a bomb disposal robot roaming between three white trucks. The rear doors of two of the vans were open and large black items could be seen scattered around. The robot appeared to be working toward getting access to the third truck.

Police gave no details as to the nationality of those arrested. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act 2000 can be detained for up to 14 days without charge, compared to the 24-hour limit for standard arrests, without an extension application.

"We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody," said Vicki Evans, the Met's counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator.

Evans said a 400-meter (yard) cordon has been put in place around the three vehicles that raised suspicion while the army conducts examinations. As a precaution, around 85 households have been evacuated whilst these examinations take place. Some have been taken to a nearby recreation center.

U.S. President Donald Trump heaped praise on those involved with the arrests.

"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."

And British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he knew the incident would be "deeply concerning" for many. In a post on social media, Burnham thanked police and the armed forces for their response and said he was grateful to the residents who have been evacuated from their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."

He urged people "not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts."

The defense secretaries of the U.S. and the U.K., Pete Hegseth and Wes Streeting, have spoken about the incident.

Under the terms agreed, the U.K. government allowed the American military to use Fairford purely for defensive purposes, such as striking Iranian missile sites.

British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the U.K., with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50% in the six months to December 2025.

The local Gloucestershire police force said the situation appeared to be "contained" and urged local residents to follow the advice as the investigation continues.

Julian Tudsbery, who has lived in Whelford for 30 years, said a resident had reported three "suspicious vans" in the village early Sunday.

"There were several police, three police cars in the drive, and they said you need to evacuate, there's been a major incident, said he couldn't elaborate," he said.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said U.S. and British personnel "remain vigilant" and will take appropriate actions to ensure safety of all those at the base.

"For operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures," the spokesperson said. "We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."

title: From ruin to a (Red) Bull market - how Prem became hot property
description: Prem Rugby seemed on the brink of disaster after Worcester, Wasps and London Irish went bust, but there is renewed confidence and fresh money in the league.
fullText:
Simon Massie-Taylor pulled up outside Newcastle's Kingston Park stadium, and saw fear.

The unannounced arrival of Prem Rugby's chief executive at one of the league's clubs had rarely been a good sign.

Massie-Taylor started the role in January 2022. In the 18 months that followed, Wasps, Worcester and London Irish, with finances stretched out of shape by Covid, had flamed out of the English top flight.

"When those clubs were going into administration, the common denominator was their leadership leaving the room," remembers Massie-Taylor.

"The owners, the chief executives, everyone went.

"So it was basically up to me, [Rugby Players Association general secretary] Christian Day and [Rugby Football Union director of legal and governance] Angus Bujalski to go in and say, 'we're terribly sorry, this is what's happened, this is what it means for you'.

"Telling anyone that they've lost their job is one of the worst bits of having a job. But when it comes to sport, for the people that work in those clubs, it's not just a job, it's a way of life. It was horrible."

So when Massie-Taylor pitched up at Newcastle last year, with the club limping from payroll to payroll, onlookers feared the worse.

"Some of the players and staff, when they first saw me, thought I was this grim reaper figure coming to deliver another bad news story," he said.

Instead he ushered Newcastle's staff into a room decked out in the blue and silver branding of Red Bull.

Backed by a hype video filled with signature extreme sport stunts, executives from the energy drink giant, fresh off a flight, spelled out a grand vision for the Prem's bottom club.

"There were people in that room in tears, it was pretty special," said Massie-Taylor.

That investment was a pivot point for the league.

Massie-Taylor remembers how low the bar was to buy into the Prem in his first few, stressful years. "It was 'do you exist, have you got a criminal record, do you actually have any money?," he says.

But Red Bull's arrival, sealed and delivered in August 2025, marked a sea change.

Since then Black Knight - the owners of Premier League side Bournemouth - have bought up Exeter Chiefs, billionaire industrialist Sir James Dyson has taken a 50% share of Bath and financier Steve Zander has made a multi-million pound investment into Northampton Saints., external

More outside investment is expected soon, with Gloucester and Leicester among those in conversations.

"Investor interest in the league has increased significantly in the last 12 months, certainly the last six," says Massie-Taylor, who convened a summit for prospective buyers in London in June and is heading to the United States in October to press flesh and make the case.

His confidence is shared by more impartial experts.

Matthew Wheeler helped broker Red Bull's takeover of Newcastle, but his specialist investment group A&W Capital has made deals across a variety of sports and media.

"I don't think you're drunk from the Kool-Aid to have belief in the Prem, there definitely is a momentum behind it," he says.

Andrew Umbers is a co-founder of Oakwell Sports Advisory, which had a similar role in Exeter's takeover.

"We put Exeter in front just over 110 sports investors and we had interest probably from around 30," he says. "That interest came from North America, Asia and continental Europe."

It is quite the difference from when Massie-Taylor would entertain enquiries from anyone with proof of identity, a clean chargesheet and a positive bank balance.

There are a few factors that are happy coincidence, rather than canny design.

The value of sports teams generally has risen steeply. The sale of the LA Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.3bn) this summer is the prime example.

Wheeler puts the spike down to the guaranteed eyeballs sport attracts in a fragmented media world, its relative resistance to disruption by artificial intelligence as a product and the prestige and scarcity value of owning a sports team.

Prem Rugby was also on an upward growth trajectory before the Covid pandemic hit. Even with the loss of three teams, a return to normality has allowed the league to rediscover that groove.

A brand of the heft of Red Bull getting involved in the league, undoubtedly sparked interest elsewhere.

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

However, proactive changes have played a part.

An independent financial monitoring panel has kept across all Prem club finances for the past couple of seasons, and is designed to prevent dangerous levels of risk and spending. That has reassured investors.

With a funding deal with the Rugby Football Union and broadcast partnership with TNT Sports locked in for several seasons, there is stability for the foreseeable.

A calendar shift, external has meant England internationals are available more often to their clubs, raising the wattage on the domestic game's star power.

And, while Massie-Taylor won't say it himself, he has inspired confidence. A former investment banker, he understands what prospective buyers are looking for.

"He's done a good job," says Wheeler.

"The governance is important because the first thing an investor wants to know is can they rely on the management and is the league going to be well run.

"You may be buying into an individual team, but you're really buying into the league.

"You can have the most successful team you want, but if the league's not successful, it doesn't mean anything."

Massie-Taylor's most important decision might be his most controversial.

He backed the ring-fencing of the league, scrapping relegation and bringing new teams in via a tender process rather than achievements on the pitch.

This season is the first to be played out without even a hint of jeopardy at the bottom of the table.

It has been unpopular with fans.

While some see a betrayal of sporting tradition, the change gives Prem Rugby a point of difference over lower-level football sides competing for the same investment.

No possible drop down the leagues, no danger of a distressed asset.

"It is a real thing for US investors," says Massie-Taylor.

"There was a fear and, to some extent, a handbrake on investment because of that financial jeopardy."

It is just one aspect of the league that makes prospective American buyers comfortable.

The upper and, from this season, lower limits on how much Prem clubs can spend on players' salaries are common in Stateside sport, as is the equitable sharing of media revenues.

There has also been a shift to centralise deals and maximise revenues.

A proposal to have one kit manufacturer for the whole league - something seen in America's 'big four' leagues (NBA, NFL, MLB and NHL) - has been floated in the past.

"For an investor, owning a Prem Rugby team is more is more like owning an NFL team than it is like owning a Premier League football team [in that regard]," says Wheeler.

It was noticeable that Brett Gosper, formerly the head of World Rugby, now leading NFL Europe, was on hand at Prem Rugby's investor summit to underline those parallels.

The combination of features of a franchise league, with the long rivalries and established, loyal fanbases that a start-up competition lacks, makes the Prem a rare prospect.

"American investors are interested in under-commercialised sport, below the tier-one leagues such as Premier League, NFL or the IPL, that are at a turning point in their cycle," says Umbers.

"We think Prem Rugby is one of those."

"Rugby is not a big sport in America, so there has got to be some education going on," he says.

"But will American investors be interested once they understand the dynamics? Yes."

Massie-Taylor knows the margins are narrow.

A 10-team league cannot afford any more clubs to go under. There are financial debts and a dependency on owner generosity across the league.

But he heads to America with momentum.

"We've proved there's opportunity going forward," he says.

"The thing that's niggling us now is the fear that we don't make the most of it. That's the pressure we all feel to really crack on."

It isn't just the players aiming to start the season fast.

fullText:
In the choreographers’ new work, virtuosic movement and some green-screen magic unfurl the theatricality of high-stakes television interviews

It appears the interviewer has got him on the ropes. “For the record, I did not take part in a pagan ceremony with minor members of the royal family in which we daubed ourselves in paint,” states the beleaguered politician, caught outside Buckingham Palace with his flies undone and forced to defend himself. This is a fabrication, of course – I’m watching the scene play out in an east London dance studio – but it doesn’t feel miles away from something that could be true. And how do we know what’s the truth anyway? That’s the question in Deepfake, the latest piece from award-winning dance duo Jessica Wright and Morgann Runacre-Temple, AKA Jess and Morgs.

The pair tell modern stories with ambitious tech – film and live camera work – and often techy themes, too. “We’ve always been drawn to where there’s a crossover between the theme and the form,” says Runacre-Temple. “What gets us excited is seeing the contemporary world reflected back.” The pair scored a massive hit with their 2022 piece Coppélia, made for Scottish Ballet, which turned a twee 19th-century ballet about a dancing doll into a cautionary tale of AI automatons and unrestrained tech bro egos. Definitely not one-hit wonders, earlier this year they made their debut at the highly esteemed Paris Opera Ballet.

Deepfake is set in a green-screen studio, where the interview is taking place between a cool-headed journalist and a politician. With writer Jeff James, Jess and Morgs looked at a wealth of TV interviews, from Jeremy Paxman’s 1997 grilling of Michael Howard, where he asked the same question 12 times, to the former prince Andrew’s disastrous turn on Newsnight. They also took inspiration from the current ultra-media-trained politicos who “continually and bombastically evade any questions at all”, says Wright.

They liked the way the television interview is already a theatrical setup, says Wright. “I think there’s something fun about putting that on stage and asking the audience to engage with the theatricality as well.” It’s gladiatorial drama in smart tailoring. “It’s really high stakes; it’s win or lose for both of them,” adds Wright.

In the show, the interview will be filmed live by four cameras – then, as well as seeing what’s happening in reality, the audience will watch another version on screen with background footage edited in. We’ll be privy to the fabrication of the image and a number of possible realities. There are also seven dancers in green-screen suits who manipulate the environment but will disappear in the edit.

As Runacre-Temple says, green screen can actually look quite lo-fi – “It’s got that slightly absurd, playful, silent movie quality about it” – and it’s ancient tech compared with the kind of AI deepfakes that are emerging today. “They look so hyper real,” says Runacre-Temple. “The danger of deepfakes is not only that people believe things that aren’t true to be real, but that they start to disbelieve things that are true, and this gap opens up of doubt and scepticism about everything.” Or, as in their story, someone who has been caught out doing something they shouldn’t can insist it’s a fake image. “It’s really about the strange shifting relationship with the landscape of truth.”

I go to visit rehearsals on a day when there’s no tech in sight, bar a couple of laptops. “It’s good to go analogue to actually finish the choreography,” says Wright, wryly, counting the diminishing days to the premiere. All we have is an enormous studio and two incredible dancers: Rebecca Bassett-Graham, best known for dancing with Wayne McGregor’s company, who is playing the journalist; and as the politician, Kennedy Junior Muntanga, who has worked with Akram Khan.

The text plays in voiceover while the two dancers embody and expand on its meaning. Their quick-fire movements visualise all the dynamics of a charged conversation: charm, challenge, cooperation, accusation, entrapment, etc. The feel is freewheeling, but each movement is tightly mapped to the syllable, every flex of muscle is considered. In certain scenes with the green screen, dancers will have to hit exact marks and even eyelines on exact words “or the whole illusion collapses”, says Wright. They’re creating their own high-stakes environment for the performers, where “the dancers’ virtuosity is a metaphor for these very virtuosic performances in interviews”.

Will this battle have a winner? Can we believe what we see? Jess and Morgs aren’t giving any spoilers. “Hopefully it will be surprising and mischievous,” says Runacre-Temple.
