title: 'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
description: The London City Lionesses raised eyebrows with no English players in their starting line-up against Manchester United, but is there a wider trend?
fullText:
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.

For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.

Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.

Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.

But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?

Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?

Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League

Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST

Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns

Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.

In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.

As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.

Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.

The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.

"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.

"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."

Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.

The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.

It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.

For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.

And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.

"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.

"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."

Ellen White and Ben Haines discuss homegrown WSL players on the Women's Football Weekly

Superstar-led London City live up to hype as Man Utd suffer

It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.

After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.

Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.

Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.

Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.

Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.

It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.

Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.

When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.

Young Lionesses win European trophy

To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.

The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.

Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."

"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.

"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"

Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".

The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.

Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.

title: British player receives surprise Laver Cup call-up for London event
description: The last edition at The O2 in 2022 saw three-time Grand Slam champion Andy Murray compete for Team Europe
fullText:
British No 1 Arthur Fery has been called up as a Team Europe alternate for this weekend's Laver Cup in London.

Fery, who reached the semi-finals of Wimbledon in July and led the British side that defeated Ecuador in the Davis Cup at the Copper Box Arena over the weekend, will serve as a back-up to Yannick Noah's six-strong team at The O2 this weekend.

The 24-year-old will practice with the team – which consists of Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Flavio Cobolli, Rafael Jodar, Jakub Mensik and Casper Ruud – and will fill in should there be an injury or withdrawal.

"It's an honour to be part of Team Europe at Laver Cup, especially here at home in London," said Fery. "I grew up going to The O2, so to come back as part of Team Europe in front of the British fans is something I'm really proud of and am looking forward to.

"It's going to be great to be around some of the best players in the world and learn from them. I'll be ready to do whatever is required of me to support my teammates from the bench."

At the last Laver Cup held in London in 2022, memorable for Roger Federer's final professional match, three-time Grand Slam finalist Andy Murray featured for Team Europe.

Team World have also named Peruvian player Ignacio Buse, the world No 35, as an alternate to back up Alex de Minaur, Taylor Fritz, Brandon Nakashima, Alexander Bublik, Learner Tien and Francisco Cerundolo. Nakashima replaced Ben Shelton in the visiting team's line-up after the US Open finalist withdrew last week.

"Laver Cup is a historic event and I'm very excited to be part of it," said Buse. "It's an incredible opportunity to be surrounded by so many great players and icons of the sport and to have someone with Andre Agassi's experience as a coach.

"I'm going to enjoy it, learn as much as I can and make the most of the experience."

This week's event in London will be the ninth Laver Cup in total, after the tournament debuted in Prague in 2017.

Team World have won three of the last four events, after Team Europe won the first four editions.

title: Why Cardiff is set to win race to host Fury-Joshua
description: Why Cardiff is set to beat competition from London and New York to host the long-awaited fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua.
fullText:
The long-awaited heavyweight fight between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua is expected to take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on Friday, 11 December.

While BBC Sport understands final details are still being hammered out between Netflix, Saudi Arabian organisers Sela and both fighters' camps, Cardiff has firmly emerged as the frontrunner, with an official announcement expected this week.

It marks another dramatic twist in a saga that, only weeks ago, appeared destined for New York. A date at Madison Square Garden was so close to completion that plans were already being drawn up for a Manhattan news conference.

Instead, after Joshua and promoter Eddie Hearn refused to budge on their contractual right to stage the fight on British soil, the Welsh capital has taken centre stage.

BBC Sport takes a look at how Cardiff became the leading candidate to host what would arguably be the biggest event in British boxing in the 21st Century.

Wembley Stadium was long assumed to be the natural home for a meeting between the two defining British heavyweights of their generation. However, the path to making the fight was complicated by Joshua and Fury having signed separate agreements with Sela rather than a joint contract.

Joshua's deal explicitly stipulated that the bout must take place in the United Kingdom, whereas Fury's contained no such restriction.

That distinction proved critical when organisers and broadcast partner Netflix began lobbying to move the show to the United States.

Hearn acknowledged that virtually every other party involved preferred New York, with Matchroom even exploring what compensation would be required to waive the UK clause.

For a moment, that stand-off threatened to scupper the entire event. Fury publicly accused Joshua of stalling and briefly floated the prospect of a trilogy fight with Oleksandr Usyk.

But once Fury relented, organisers needed to find a British venue capable of satisfying the broadcast demands without leaving fans exposed to the British winter.

Cardiff, almost by process of elimination, became the answer.

The fight had initially been discussed for November but, with negotiations over the venue dragging on, it now looks set for December.

Staging an open-air stadium fight in the UK at that time carries immense risk.

While Wembley offers unmatched prestige, exposing tens of thousands of fans and a massive international broadcast operation to potentially freezing temperatures, wind and rain was deemed unacceptable.

Moving the event indoors to an arena like London's O2 would eliminate weather risks, but at the cost of sacrificing tens of thousands of ticket sales.

The Principality Stadium's retractable roof allows organisers to capture the immense scale, atmosphere and gate revenue of a stadium show while offering full protection from the elements.

The venue's official seated capacity is just under 74,000, but boxing configurations allow for even larger crowds.

Joshua has already proven he can sell out the venue, having defended his WBA and IBF titles there against Carlos Takam in front of nearly 80,000 fans in 2017 before adding the WBO belt against Joseph Parker five months later.

'Bring it on' - Cardiff businesses react to Fury vs Joshua rumours

Perhaps the most difficult hurdle has been aligning the event with Netflix's preference to broadcast during prime-time hours in the United States.

A projected UK ring walk of about 01:00 GMT - 20:00 on the US east coast - created a logistical headache for London. Wembley operates under a strict 23:00 event curfew.

While Mayor of London Sadiq Khan offered his support and Wembley officials were open to discussions, securing the necessary approvals from Brent Council and local safety advisory groups for a 01:00 start presented an administrative hurdle.

Cardiff offers a far smoother path. The Welsh Rugby Union, which owns and operates the Principality Stadium, previously indicated it would be delighted to host the fight and confirmed a late-night finish would not be a dealbreaker.

While early-hours finishes still require extensive coordination around transport, policing and crowd management in the city centre, the venue already holds a clear precedent for late-night boxing. In 2007, Joe Calzaghe's super-middleweight unification victory over Mikkel Kessler did not start until 02:00 local time to satisfy American television network Showtime.

For all the delays and frustrations that have plagued this rivalry over the past decade, Fury against Joshua remains the pinnacle of domestic boxing. Downgrading to an indoor arena would diminish the magnitude of the occasion.

Crucially, taking the fight to America would have deprived domestic fans of a generational spectacle. British supporters have driven the commercial value of this rivalry for years, filling stadiums for both fighters' respective careers and following every collapsed negotiation.

Staging the bout on home soil serves as a long-overdue reward for that loyalty, even if both men are now former world heavyweight champions.

A stadium fight of this magnitude dominates the national conversation in a way a 04:00 New York or Las Vegas broadcast simply cannot, and local amateur boxing clubs could see a surge in interest when the country's biggest stars compete on home soil.

Wales also has history of staging a huge fight between two British heavyweights: In 1993, Lennox Lewis defended his WBC title against Frank Bruno at Cardiff Arms Park - the venue that the Principality Stadium replaced.

When the demands surrounding the event are broken down, Cardiff's emergence becomes easier to understand.

title: GB reach Davis Cup Finals as Patten and Skupski win
description: Great Britain will play in the Davis Cup Finals for the first time since 2023 after taking an unassailable 3-0 lead against Ecuador in London.
fullText:
Great Britain will play in November's Davis Cup Finals as Henry Patten and Neal Skuspki won their doubles match to give the nation an unassailable 3-0 lead in their qualifying tie against Ecuador.

Toby Samuel and Arthur Fery both triumphed in their singles matches at a sold-out Copper Box Arena in London on Saturday to get Britain off to a winning start in the best-of-five tie.

Patten and Skupski then took to the court on Sunday and booked Britain's ticket to the 'Final 8' event in Bologna at the earliest opportunity with a 6-3 6-4 win over Gonzalo Escobar and Diego Hidalgo.

It is the first time that Great Britain have reached the knockout stage of the competition since 2023.

"Three years - it feels like quite a long time," Britain's captain Leon Smith told BBC Sport.

"To do it in three straight rubbers is really good and I'm actually delighted for the guys to look forward to something at the end of the year."

Even against underdogs Ecuador, whose singles players were both ranked outside of the world's top 200, there were doubts if Smith could lead Britain back to the knockout stages given his inexperienced team in London.

Jack Draper ended his difficult season early, while Jan Choinski and Jacob Fearnley were both unavailable through injury.

Smith was then dealt a late blow when British number two Cameron Norrie pulled out on Friday after feeling pain in his arm during a practice session.

However, Samuel - after a breakthrough season that has seen him rise from outside the world's top 250 to 95th in the rankings - stepped up on his Davis Cup debut.

Just weeks after winning his first Grand Slam match at the US Open, the 24-year-old overcame nerves and fought back from a set down to beat Andres Andrade 4-6 6-4 6-1.

Fery, meanwhile, was making just his second Davis Cup appearance as the British number one claimed an assured 7-5 6-0 win over Alvaro Guillen Meza.

And with world number one Patten and new US Open champion Skupski to call upon for Sunday's doubles rubber, victory seemed to be well within Britain's grasp.

The pair, despite not playing together on the ATP Tour, combined effortlessly and did not face a single break point against the Ecuadorians.

"We are good friends off the court, which I think always helps, and we spend time with each other when we are on the tour anyway," Patten told BBC Sport.

"[LTA coach] Louis Cayer has created the British system so it's quite easy for Brits to play together - we both have a good idea of what the other player is going to do, where they are going to hit it, where they are going to move to."

The last time Britain made it to the quarter-finals in 2023, they fell to a 2-0 defeat by Novak Djokovic's Serbia, with Norrie and Draper both losing their singles matches.

"When you get to the Final 8 and you play one of the seeded teams, they are extremely strong," Smith said.

"[Italy's Jannik] Sinner could be back playing, [Spain's Carlos] Alcaraz has talked about his commitment to it at the end of the year, but you've got a chance. You try and steal one of the singles, and it goes to the doubles and you've got a good doubles team.

"There's a lot of excitement about it, it brings the team together again."

Three-time defending champions Italy qualified automatically as hosts for the Finals, which will take place in in Bologna from 24 to 29 November.

But the United States, who have won a record 32 Davis Cup titles, will be absent from the quarter-finals for a second successive year after they fell to a 3-2 defeat by the Czech Republic.

Christian Harrison and Austin Krajicek won their doubles match to give the Americans a 2-1 lead, but US Open runner-up Ben Shelton lost to Jakub Mensik before Jiri Lehecka sealed the tie for the Czechs with victory over Learner Tien.

South Korea advanced to the knockout stage for the first time on Saturday after beating India 3-1, while Austria joined them with a win over Belgium.

Canada, the 2022 champions, are also through after a 3-1 victory against France, while US Open champion Alexander Zverev won both his singles matches to help Germany to a 3-1 win over Croatia.

Spain are 2-0 up against Chile, with their qualifying tie resuming at 15:00 BST on Sunday.

title: 'Fragile' Tottenham beaten by Aston Villa despite late rally
description: The end to Tottenham's Premier League goal drought came too late as Aston Villa won 3-2 in north London on Saturday to compound a miserable start for Roberto De Zerbi's men.Without a league win this season, Tottenham are off to their worst start in the Premier League era and only netted their first goals of the campaign after the visitors had surged into a 3-0 lead.
fullText:
The end to Tottenham's Premier League goal drought came too late as Aston Villa won 3-2 in north London on Saturday to compound a miserable start for Roberto De Zerbi's men.

Without a league win this season, Tottenham are off to their worst start in the Premier League era and only netted their first goals of the campaign after the visitors had surged into a 3-0 lead.

Villa had also struggled for goals themselves since the side that won the Europa League last season was torn apart during the transfer window.

But new signings Johan Manzambi and Nicolas Jackson struck either side of half-time before Emi Buendia's wonder strike to give Unai Emery's new-look team their first league win.

"Competing like we did, winning like we did will give us confidence collectively and individually, it is really very important," said Emery.

"We are delighted because we needed it and we were suffering in the Premier League."

Even Tottenham's first late consolation needed the aid of a Villa deflection when Conor Gallagher's effort went in off Matty Cash before Jan Paul van Hecke headed home in stoppage time.

Spurs splashed out over £300 million ($400 million) on new players to try and avoid a repeat of the battle for survival they endured last season.

Yet there remains little return on that investment.

"I want to say is that we played well in the first half, we didn't score, but (we are ) too fragile," said De Zerbi.

"The moment when we have to defend, we have to defend compact. The leaders have to be leaders and to lead the team."

In keeping with recent performances, Spurs started brightly before fizzling out.

Twice in a matter of seconds Savio was kept out by Suzuki before the Japanese goalkeeper spread himself to turn behind Archie Gray's powerful strike.

Villa had picked up just one point from their opening four league games but have missed their club record signing Manzambi for most of that period.

The Swiss international opened his Villa account when he tapped home Boubacar Kamara's cross.

De Zerbi described Tottenham's defending for the second goal as "incredible" and not in a good sense as Van Hecke failed to deal with a long ball straight down the middle.

Jackson did well to evade the Dutch defender and then fired down into the ground and past Antonin Kinsky.

The Czech goalkeeper was powerless to stop Villa's third 11 minutes from time when Buendia took aim from long range and brilliantly picked out the top corner.

A chorus of boos greeted Buendia's strike as thousands of home fans headed for an early exit.

But those that left missed finally have something to celebrate.

Fine persistence from Mohammed Kudus teed up Gallagher to find the bottom corner via the outstretched foot of Cash.

Van Hecke then bulleted in from Andy Robertson's free-kick with virtually the last touch of the game.

Spurs now must stew on another defeat for a three-week international break while rooted in the relegation zone.

Villa, by contrast, will hope victory can prove the catalyst to storm up the table as they did last season.

Emery's men failed to win any of their first five league games a year ago, but ultimately finished fourth.

title: London City's new training centre 'better than most Premier League clubs' - Kang
description: Michele Kang believes London City Lionesses' planned new training ground will set a new standard in the women's game and surpass facilities used by most men's Premier League clubs.
fullText:
Michele Kang believes London City Lionesses' planned training ground will set a new standard in the women's game and surpass facilities used by the majority of men's Premier League clubs.

Over the summer, Kang boosted the Women's Super League side with significant investment in players, including the signing of two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Kang revealed a purpose-built training centre is expected to open within the next year.

She said: "We're building a state-of-the-art training centre for our female athletes dedicated to them, built and designed for them, which will open in less than a year.

"Our architect, who has built several Premier League training centres told me that by the time the London City training centre is up and running, it would be better than with the majority of Premier League men's teams training centres."

Kang views investment in infrastructure as part of a wider remit to ensure female athletes are no longer treated differently from their male counterparts.

"How could you possibly accept the notion that your girls, your daughters, granddaughters, sisters are treated as second-class citizens where in the same sport the boys go to play as if it's their birthright?"

She believes that for too long, women have been treated like "small men".

"We have to take care of our female players better so that they can train, perform, and thrive as female athletes, not small men," she said.

"You drive your boy to a state-of-the-art training centre and then, if you're lucky enough to have a facility nearby, you drive your girl somewhere else. Why would you accept that?"

Kang is a strong advocate of independent women's clubs and said that was one of the reasons she was attracted to London City Lionesses.

"My first entree into women's football was Washington Spirit, in the United States, where two thirds of women's teams are independent and not affiliated with men's team. So to me, that's a lot more normal.

"I wanted to show that there isn't just one model that the women's team has to be part of the men's team, but an independent team, because I think at that time, London City and Durham, if I'm not mistaken, those are the two, women-only teams.

"I wanted to build a women-only team to show when you really devote all your attention and resources and energy into women's only team, what's possible."

Kang traces much of that belief back to her upbringing in South Korea and the influence of her father.

When asked why she is so passionate about women, Kang said: "I think it probably originally came from my father. From very early on, my father, who had only three girls. It maybe was a necessity.

"I was growing up in South Korea, where it was still a very traditional society, where girls have certain roles.

"He said in this day and age it doesn't matter whether you're a girl or a boy, whatever you want to do, you have to put 100% of what you have and you can go for it. And if you don't achieve, you have only yourself to blame."

Kang says those lessons have stayed with her throughout her career.

"I'm grateful that I achieved my American dream. And this is my way of giving back that I don't want, quite frankly, a lot of young girls growing up going through what I went through.

"I want them to be able to focus on what they have to do to be the best football player, not having to worry about changing clothes in the middle of a public park or broken equipment - all those type of things."

The club's training centre is also expected to support research into female athlete health, an area Kang believes has been overlooked for decades. Kang pointed to injury rates as one example.

"There are more ACL, injuries among female players. The tune of two or three times more female players get ACL injuries than male players," she said.

"Something like 94% of all science medical research is dedicated to men. So there's just fundamentally so little known about female body."

Kang's ambitions extend beyond London. Through her multi-club ownership model, which already spans England, France and the United States, she wants the standards being established at London City to be replicated across the globe.

"I would like to buy a team in Asia. I would like to buy a team in Africa. I would like to buy a team in South America, because I want all the girls in those countries to grow up thinking that this kind of the best, best, facilities and best practices and unbelievably, infrastructure is not something that they can only watch on TV because they're only in England, France, America, but it's in their backyard."

The owner says she wants future generations of female players to enjoy opportunities equal to those available to boys, regardless of where they grow up.

"That reality, the gap between the girls and boys journeys is indefensible, and I want that to disappear."

And when asked what message she had for the rest of the Women's Super League, her answer was short and direct.

title: London Lions set for NBA test as British basketball bids to step up
description: The 2026-27 Super League Basketball season gets under way on Friday - and could be the most competitive in a generation, according to Newcastle Eagles owner Paul Blake.
fullText:
"I've been involved for 30 years now and it's definitely the most competitive it's been, pretty much in all those 30 years," Newcastle Eagles owner Paul Blake said.

Excitement is building as British men's top-flight basketball prepares for a new season - with champions London Lions gearing up for a prestigious friendly against NBA opposition in Portland Trail Blazers next month.

Before that, though, the third season of the men's Super League Basketball - launched in 2024 after the British Basketball League folded - begins on Friday, as the Lions head to Bristol Flyers.

Last season, the Lions completed a domestic quadruple by winning the SLB Championship, SLB Playoffs, SLB Cup and SLB Trophy - and will be amining for more success when the campaign concludes in May.

This season, there will be 10 teams - up from nine - following the addition of Liverpool Basketball.

SLBW, the women's competition, starts on Saturday, 3 October.

For many SLB clubs, there is optimism going into the new campaign - given some fine recent results and performances.

Manchester Basketball became the first British team to win a qualifying round match in Fiba's Basketball Champions League by beating German side Wurzburg Baskets earlier this week.

Bristol Flyers, meanwhile, will again compete in the European North Basketball League (ENBL), a competition in which Manchester finished runners-up last season.

The Lions are back in the EuroCup for a second straight season, EuroLeague's second-tier European club basketball competition - and are in good spirits after beating EuroLeague outfit Paris Basketball in pre-season earlier this month.

"The league is just getting more and more competitive all the time, so we know we'll be in for a fight again this season," Eagles owner Blake, who is also an SLB director, told BBC Sport.

"The quality of players that are now in the league across the teams top to bottom is, for me, pretty much the highest level it's been. It's extremely competitive."

The Lions want to become one of world basketball's most recognisable clubs.

On 12 October, they will become the first British side to play an NBA team, when they face a friendly in the USA against the Portland Trail Blazers.

"I've wanted to be in the NBA since I was six years old. This is the closest I've ever been," Lions CEO Lenz Balan told BBC Sport.

"It's a really important signal in the basketball world, in the sporting world. This is the ambition. We are absolutely trying to be one of the best clubs in the world."

As well as looking to defend a domestic quadruple, the Lions will hope to improve on last season's EuroCup campaign.

While they did beat eventual runners-up Besiktas Gain in the group stage, they ultimately finished eighth out of 10 teams.

Balan is hopeful that their summer acquisitions, including the loan arrival of 2025-26 EuroLeague winner Keenan Evans, will help the Lions compete in Europe.

"We have ambitions to definitely outperform last year," added Balan.

"It's going to be tough, but these are some of the best players in the world - and I think most people in London and the UK recognise the level of competition that they're playing.

"We're just really focused on executing that vision, getting better and if we keep doing that, I think we're going to get some good results."

Just 15 days after the SLB season tips off, SLBW will do the same.

Cardiff Met Archers host B Braun Sheffield Hatters, the defending championship and play-off winners, in the opening match on Saturday, 3 October.

At Cardiff, four players are salaried while also studying masters degrees at the university.

The rest of the team are made up of players on scholarships, postgraduate and undergraduate students and others that are balancing a career in basketball with full-time work.

"I think there's an opportunity to build something that people genuinely want to watch and follow," Archers head coach Stef Collins, a member of Great Britain's 2012 Olympic squad, told BBC Sport.

"Women's basketball has shown what is possible internationally, particularly with the growth we're seeing in leagues like the WNBA, NCAA College Basketball."

Collins wants SLBW to build on the recent Women's World Cup in Berlin, at which the United States earned a fifth successive title, beating France in the final.

"It was the most-attended World Cup in the modern era with over 230,000 fans in attendance," she said.

"For me, it's also about telling the stories of the players. They're not just basketball players - they're students, they're professionals, they're international athletes, they're role models. If we can showcase that properly, I think there's an exciting future for the Super league."

The WNBA, the independent women's equivalent of North America's NBA, has been among the pioneers in women's sports leagues across the globe.

In 2025, WNBA clips gained more than one billion views on Instagram, making it the most-followed women's sports league on that platform, which Collins feels can help SLBW on its path for development.

"The WNBA is a really good example of what happens when you give women's basketball a platform and make the players and their stories visible," she said.

"But I think there's also a lesson beyond the basketball itself. Women's sport has shown that fans want to connect with the athletes, their personalities and their stories.

"We shouldn't be afraid to market women's basketball differently and allow our players to be themselves."

title: Sun Devils, except coach Kenny Dillingham, soaking up London ahead of Union Jack Classic
description: LONDON – Featuring ornate, architectural marvels and historic sites dating back centuries, this isn’t a city that should be explored in a hotel room – unless you’re Arizona State football...
fullText:
LONDON – Featuring ornate, architectural marvels and historic sites dating back centuries, this isn't a city that should be explored in a hotel room – unless you're Arizona State football coach Kenny Dillingham.

After a long trip across the pond, the Sun Devils' head man said that he had spent roughly 48 hours indoors at the team hotel, sequestered in his room like a hermit to prepare for Arizona State's game at Wembley Stadium against Kansas in the Union Jack Classic on Saturday. Kickoff is at 9 a.m. MST.

With the sun peeking through gray London skies, Dillingham finally caught a whiff of fresh outside air at ASU's Tuesday morning practice. Don't get any ideas. Dillingham said it won't be happening much this week, at least when it comes to non-team-related activities.

"I didn't sleep the first 36 hours I was here," Dillingham said. "I've been locked in a cave.

"My job is to get the best plan in place, and I (have) got to do the same process I do throughout a week. … We'll go to the Thursday event that we (have) got down there in London, but I don't plan on doing anything other than being in this hotel."

While Dillingham isn't keen to explore the city, he has encouraged his team to enjoy the unique experience of playing in an international game – a historic one at that, considering that it's the first-ever college football game in London to feature two FBS teams.

"I told them today, they're not hostages here," Dillingham said. "If you want to go do something, go do something. Just make sure we get what we need to get accomplished."

It's been a taxing turnaround for Dillingham's squad. Fresh off a 48-20 loss in College Station to No. 9 Texas A&M on Sept. 12, the Sun Devils flew straight to London for the back half of a roughly week-and-a-half-long stretch on the road.

The trip presents some obvious logistical hurdles – shipping a football team and its gear thousands of miles away isn't a straightforward task. Conversely, it provides ASU's players and staff with a chance to escape from football and create memorable moments as a team.

"No way would I want our team to fly across the country Week 3 to play this game," Dillingham said. "But this is an experience. They're still college athletes and I wasn't going to rob them of an experience to fly them across the country, go see London, be able to experience things and play in a stadium that's like a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

Veterans such as offensive tackle Jalen Klemm and defensive tackle C.J. Fite have kept busy, visiting local landmarks and trying one of England's most popular dishes for the first time: fish and chips.

"We have been taking the last couple of days to kind of acclimate to everything," Klemm said. "All of us have walked the grounds here and looked at everything. I know that on Thursday we have a boat ride that we're going to be able to go on and see a lot of the sights. So I know the guys are pretty excited for that."

For the most part, Dillingham has entrusted his players with the freedom to explore London on their own. Well, at least with a buddy. Or three.

Behind the program's pillars – which include, Fite noted being a good person and having safeguards like the buddy system in place – older players such as Fite and Klemm haven't felt the need to heavily monitor the younger players to prevent them from making poor decisions.

"Coach told us if you want to go out, you have to have three people with you," Fite said. "So if somebody wants to make a bad decision, three other people can stop them. There's certain things that you do, and that you already know, that kind of stop you from making those decisions. But all the guys kind of know already."

Like any trip abroad, it hasn't been smooth sailing for everyone. Klemm said his teammate, sophomore offensive lineman Manamo'ui Muti, found himself in a precarious position early in the week: locked in the hotel bathroom.

"It was pretty funny," Klemm said. "We went in there and we were knocking on the door and he was like, 'Hey guys,' and he was sending us videos from inside.

"Thankfully, he had his phone. I asked him what he would have done if he didn't have his phone. He was like, 'I might have had to break the door down.'"

While it seems the Devils are enjoying their time across the pond, they still remain aligned with their uber-focused coach, pledging not to let distractions get in the way of their main goal.

"At the end of the day, we came here to play a football game," Klemm said. "We got to keep the main thing the main thing."

title: ‘I created my mom and talk to her’: AI ghosts and deathslop are changing the way we mourn
description:
The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation
Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity.
fullText:
The rise of AI-generated tributes and bots for ‘talking’ to the dead has experts concerned more people will grieve in isolation

Tributes rolled in after the death of Dolly Parton last month. Jack White performed Jolene at a London gig. Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. Even Pitbull stopped his Madison Square Garden show to memorialize Parton and all the other “powerful women” in the crowd. But one of the strangest – and most viral – eulogies did not come from a celebrity. It did not even come from a person.

Run Jolene, at just under five minutes, is an earworm of a country song, containing all the cliches of the genre: twangy singer, banjo licks, corny lyrics. Those lyrics concern Jolene, the fictional romantic rival made infamous by Parton. “Somebody better warn Jolene / Dolly’s coming through those gates,” the voice croons. “Run Jolene / Girl you better move your feet.”

The accompanying video depicts Parton, clad in a bedazzled white jumpsuit, hunting down Jolene, a busty redhead with prom curls. Heaven is filled with deceased celebrities who watch on in horror – or amusement – as Jolene bounces from cloud to cloud, or books it up marble staircases, trying to hide from Dolly. Onlookers include the late Michael Jackson, Whitney Houston and Kenny Rogers, as well as Cher, who is still very much alive.

On TikTok, YouTube and Spotify, the song credit is Country Mile, an “artist” with just over 6,000 monthly listeners (that’s not many). The project is textbook AI slop, seemingly released by an anonymous creator who calls their work “genre fluid ai vibes”. But Run Jolene is not so universally panned: clips have been viewed more than 1.4m times on TikTok, with commenters raving: “I don’t give a flying fuck if this is AI or not! THIS IS FUCKING COOL!!”, “this is fun …think Dolly would love it ❤️”, and “Who says Jolene’s up there.”

Run Jolene is only one part of a ghoulish online ecosystem of content dubbed “deathslop”. Anyone can create deathslop: all it takes is access to an AI image generator and the time required to type in a prompt. Creators have shown Parton alongside a chummy Charlie Kirk and George Floyd, who welcome her as their “new neighbor” in the afterlife, or having tea with the Golden Girls.

These tributes pop up quickly, reducing someone’s legacy to cheap content that panders for views. It is a dishonest portrayal at best, and inflicts pain at its worst. The phenomenon inspired Parton’s grieving family to beg users to quit it with the “fake AI garbage” and “misinformation”. “It’s been challenging to absorb and or ignore,” Stella Parton, her sister, wrote on Instagram.

Parton’s image now joins the likeness of other deceased figures treated to unsettling AI depictions. Coinciding with the one year anniversary of the assassination of Kirk, social media feeds have proliferated with posts featuring the AI-generated, heavy-handed (and heavily memed) anthem “We Are Charlie Kirk”. Robin Williams, Elvis Presley, Kobe Bryant and Martin Luther King have all gotten the deathslop treatment – often to the horrors of their families.

OpenAI’s image generating app, Sora, was behind many a deathslop until it shut down in April after a string of controversies such as its ability to create violent and racist imagery, its use of copyrighted characters, and other thorny legal issues. (There is a lack of legal precedent over whether or not AI companies are responsible for the content users generate on their apps; and deceased people are not protected from libel.) Countless AI video generators have since taken Sora’s place.

“It is not common practice right now to consent to an AI avatar of yourself as a part of your living will,” said Jack Manning, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student who studies what academics Meredith Ringel Morris and Jed R Brubaker call “generative ghosts”, or AI-generated characters based on loved ones. “I predict that will be something that comes up.”

Manning, who is 25, lost his sister when she was 13, before the advent of generative AI. His family struggled to find ways to honor her, often fundraising for causes that were important to her. This partly inspired Manning to study the ways people mourn digitally – which now can include AI griefbots, a more personal alternative to celebrity deathslop.

With griefbots, users upload photos and videos of their loved ones and describe personal traits and values in hopes of manufacturing a continued, living presence. The companies behind the bots charge fees and lean into their inherently macabre nature with mystical names such as Seance, Re;memory and Versona.

It is also possible to command an LLM owned by ChatGPT, Claude or any number of sites for generating fantasy characters to mimic a late grandparent or deceased friend. Generative AI has hit the funeral industry too, in the form of LLMs specifically for obituary writing. One company, Treasured Memories, asks users to plug in details such as the deceased’s nickname, cause of death and hobbies, and choose the obit’s tone: “traditional”, “formal”, “witty” or “inspirational”.

Manning has never used a generative ghost to talk to his sister. It’s an issue of consent; he did not get her explicit permission to do so. Nor does he trust a bot to truly understand their relationship. “I hold these memories of her sacred, and I wouldn’t want a piece of technology to tell me I was remembering her wrong,” he said.

Justin Harrison founded Versona after his mother received a terminal cancer diagnosis. He worked on her AI replica while she was still living; she was able to see the final result and gave her approval on the project. “I totally understand why people are like, please don’t deepfake my [famous] relative once they’re dead and put them on the internet saying things they didn’t say,” Harrison said. “What we do is about personal comfort, recovery and healing. I created my mom and I talk to my mom. So it’s really nobody else’s business but my own.”

When his mom was sick, their conversations were practical in nature: “Are you talking to your dad enough? Have you gone to the doctor? Are you drinking enough water?” Harrison built the griefbot to broach more philosophical topics that they didn’t have time to discuss before she died. But four years later, Harrison does not talk to the bot all that often – maybe once a month.

“I joke that my mom’s Versona allows me to be the bad son I was never allowed to be when she was alive,” he said. “Like many busy adults, I don’t talk to her as much as I should, but I don’t have to, so it’s not the same sense of guilt.”

For Robin Silver, an ecopsychologist and death doula, these kinds of griefbots are an “unnatural method of trying to cope with a natural process”. She compared speaking to an LLM roleplaying a dead loved one to a college student asking ChatGPT to spit out a term paper. “We’re not being challenged to sit with any kind of discomfort, whether that’s the discomfort of writing an essay or the discomfort of missing someone,” she said.

Silver would instead encourage her clients to write a letter to their loved one. “I have even told people to talk to their ghosts out loud,” she said. “Meditate, or do things that they like and think of them. That’s how you keep the relationship alive in a way that is healthy, integrated and accepting the reality of your loss.”

Dr Dan Wolfson is a clinical psychologist who specializes in grief. He worries that deathbots could isolate people during a time when they need (human) support. “Having community around grief is really important,” he said. “Is AI keeping us from getting the social support that we need? Are we then not seeking to connect with our friends and family around the loss?”

AI-assisted mourning is still a niche industry; Harrison said that “thousands” of people use Versona. A June report from the estate management and planning service Empathy found that only 6% of 6,000 respondents in the US, UK and Canada reported leaning on “digital tools” such as memorial apps or griefbots for support after a death. But of those users, 88% found these tools “helpful”.

The whole conceit of a digital avatar is that it lives on for ever. It turns out that users may not need it that long. Manning says that in his research on generative ghosts, participants reported opting into these services only briefly, because they had “one last thing” to say to their loved ones: “They had a desire to say something they feel like they lost out on the chance to.”

Cathartic perhaps, but to Silver, the grief doula, these services are “a money grab”. “People will really take advantage of those in grief,” she said. “It’s a really easy time to become a mark.”

title: London loses out to Nairobi in bid to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
description: Nairobi, Kenya will be the first African host of athletics’ biggest event outside the Olympic Games
fullText:
London has lost out on hosting rights for the 2029 World Athletics Championships, with the event instead to be held in Africa for the first time.

Nairobi, Kenya submitted the winning bid, beating other candidate cities Rome, London and Munich for the rights to host athletics' biggest event outside the Olympic Games.

The hosts for the next two editions were announced in a World Athletics conference in Budapest, which has just hosted the inaugural Ultimate Championships, on Tuesday.

World Athletics president Seb Coe said "the interest in hosting our world championships has frankly never been higher" and praised "the quality, commitment and ambition demonstrated by all four... outstanding bids".

He said: "Taking our championships to Africa for the first time will be historic. Nairobi has presented a compelling and an emotional bid.

"This is a fast-growing, dynamic, modern metropolis that serves as the economic, cultural, and political hub of East Africa.

"Kenya is one of the great athletics nations. The sport is woven into the fabric of the country, and athletes such as world gold medallists Faith Kipyegon, Vivian Cheruiyot, Eliud Kipchoge, Hellen Obiri and David Rudisha, as well as two-time Olympic champion Kip Keino, multiple world cross-country champion Paul Tergat and multiple world half marathon champion Tegla Loroupe, have shaped the history of our sport.

"It was important that the World Athletics Championships should come to Africa when we had the right host, the right bid and the right circumstances. Nairobi has demonstrated emphatically that this is their moment to supercharge our sport, leaving a compelling legacy that inspires a continent."

Nairobi had submitted a bid for the 2025 edition but lost out to Tokyo, where it finished second in the medal table.

Munich was awarded host status for the 2031 edition of the biennial championships, which takes place in September at the end of the athletics season. It will be the third time Germany has hosted the event but first in the Bavarian capital.

Coe said: "Germany has proved time and again that it is an outstanding and dependable host for major athletics events. Berlin 2009 remains one of the memorable editions of the World Championships, and we have since seen tremendous support for the sport at the European Championships in Berlin and Munich."

However, the decision is a major blow to London, which had been seen as a frontrunner in the race. The UK government threw its weight behind the 2029 bid, with London Stadium - the arena purpose-built for the 2012 Olympics - intended to be the host venue.

But there were challenges even getting it off the ground in the form of needing to smooth relations with Championship football club West Ham, which had earlier argued it had priority to the stadium during the football season.

A deal was reached involving the London mayor's office, Athletic Ventures - a joint venture of UK bodies responsible for organising major events including the London Diamond League - and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which satisfied West Ham and meant the bid could go ahead. It was finally submitted last month.

But the public back-and-forth with the club was unlikely to inspire confidence in the World Athletics Council, while sparse crowds at the European Championships in Birmingham's Alexander Stadium this summer - despite being in a different city and in different circumstances - may also have damaged its standing.

Asked whether the West Ham saga played a role in London's failure, Coe refused to comment, saying: "I'm not going to maintain a running commentary today on the judgement and the basis of those judgements."

Jack Buckner, chief executive of UK Athletics and co-founder of Athletic Ventures, said: "We are deeply disappointed that the 2029 World Athletics Championships will not be held in London. We believed we had an outstanding bid which would genuinely take the sport to new levels.

"The UK is an incredible host for major sports events and the British public loves athletics. Athletic Ventures has the ambition to bring those events here and, although today's announcement hasn't gone our way, we will review and regroup. We know the world's athletes love competing here and we'll continue to explore further opportunities to make that happen.

"Our congratulations go to Nairobi and we wish the organising committee all the best for a great event in 2029."

London Stadium has not hosted an athletics championships since a highly successful 2017 edition, when Mo Farah won 10,000m gold and 5,000m silver and Britain took a surprise victory in the men's 4x100m relay. That event broke an eight-year record for ticket sales at a world championships, with more than 660,000 sold.

While the stadium has not hosted another major championships since 2017 it has welcomed the annual London Diamond League. A sellout crowd of 60,000 watched Scot Josh Kerr break the mile world record at this July's meet.

However that success was not enough to persuade World Athletics to choose the capital from the four candidates. London had specifically bid for the 2029 edition, while both Nairobi and Munich had indicated their willingness to host either in 2029 and 2031.

Beijing will host the next edition of the world championships, in 2027.

title: 'Big Ludo' - trailblazing keeper who became West Ham cult figure
description: Ludek Miklosko, who has died aged 64, was a cult figure with West Ham supporters after his move to London in 1990.
fullText:
More than a quarter of a century after he stopped playing for West Ham, the chant still regularly sung by fans shows the affection in which former Hammers goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko is held.

I play in goal for West Ham (West Ham!),

Says "Oi! Big boy! What's your name?"

Miklosko announced late in 2024 that he was withdrawing from further cancer treatment three years after his diagnosis. Days later he returned to West Ham for a Premier League match against Liverpool to a hero's reception.

On Monday, it was announced he had died at the age of 64.

No matter that his birthplace of Prostejov is about 1,000 miles from Moscow (and actually nearer London), Miklosko was a popular player who went on a trailblazing journey and won 42 international caps - the last two for the Czech Republic following Czechoslovakia's dissolution.

In a pre-internet era, Miklosko was barely known outside his homeland when he arrived in the English capital from Czech club Banik Ostrava in February 1990 as a long-term replacement for Phil Parkes in West Ham's goal.

The fall of communism had opened a path for players to leave eastern Europe for the elite leagues in the west, and after a two-month wait for a work permit during which he trained alone, he eventually became the first footballer to move from Czechoslovakia to England.

Manager Lou Macari travelled to Prague to accompany his £300,000 signing on the flight to Heathrow Airport but missed his debut, resigning a day later, with Billy Bonds taking over.

Miklosko, then aged 28, began his time in England staying in a hotel, with little grasp of English and no car, and would be given lifts to and from training by team-mates Ian Bishop and Trevor Morley.

The goalkeeper went on to become a cult figure with supporters, making 374 appearances for the Hammers over eight years, and had a spell back at the club as goalkeeping coach after ending his playing days with a three-year stint at Queens Park Rangers.

He was named the Hammer of the Year as West Ham won promotion back to the top flight in 1991 with a squad that included Julian Dicks and Frank McAvennie, and appeared in FA Cup and League Cup semi-finals.

The 6ft 5in shot-stopper will be particularly remembered for some brilliant displays in front of the old Boleyn Ground crowd.

Most memorable of all was on the final day of the 1994-95 season, when he single-handedly kept out the attacking might of Manchester United to deny them a third consecutive Premier League title.

A victory for the visitors would have given them the trophy as Blackburn lost to Liverpool, but they were held to a 1-1 draw and Rovers were crowned champions.

Miklosko stood in United's way, denying Mark Hughes, Lee Sharpe and Andy Cole in what frustrated Red Devils manager Alex Ferguson described as a "siege".

Years later, the keeper visited Manchester United's training academy, where staff recalled his efforts.

"A few of them said: 'I was there and remember that game and I hated you'. We had a good laugh about it," he told West Ham's website in 2020, saying he "never tired" of talking about that match.

Miklosko had an operation to remove a lump he discovered on his hip in 2021, and while radiotherapy initially helped with a further stomach tumour, he decided against chemotherapy for more tumours after discussions with his doctors.

He had returned to Banik Ostrava as sporting director in 2022 and wanted to carry on working. Supporters there unveiled a giant banner in support of him at a game earlier in 2025, with his picture and the words 'Big Ludo'.

"I have two football clubs in my heart - Banik Ostrava and West Ham United - and in a funny way they are very similar. Even the mentality of the fans, very similar. Hard-working people, loyal and passionate," he said,

"If I am ever doing an interview here in the Czech Republic, I am always saying this and making this comparison.

"West Ham United is my second family. After all these years, they still remember me, still sing my name, and that is a great feeling."

His name is Ludek Miklosko. He will be fondly remembered.

title: US embassy child abuse images suspect flown from UK before police interview
description: The individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south London, had diplomatic protection, despite not being a diplomat.
fullText:
A US embassy staffer accused of possessing indecent images of children, was detained at his south London flat and flown out of the UK in August, without being first questioned by British police.

The US Embassy confirmed to the BBC that authorities are investigating the allegations and they have reassigned the staff member to the US while inquiries continue.

"The United States government expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously," embassy officials said in a statement.

They added that they "quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action."

It is understood the individual worked at the US embassy in Vauxhall, south west London, and though not a diplomat, he enjoyed the umbrella of diplomatic protection.

A UK government spokesperson said: "We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas."

title: Buildings are sinking and cracking in one of Europe’s largest cities
description: As blistering temperatures baked London this summer, strange things started happening: zig-zagging cracks suddenly appeared across walls, doors got stuck, windows warped.
fullText:
As blistering temperatures baked London this summer, people started to notice strange things happening to their houses: zig-zagging cracks suddenly appeared across walls, doors got stuck, windows warped.

Extreme heat brings many problems for a country not built for it: Schools close, train tracks buckle and — it turns out — houses sink.

🌡️ Get your local forecast from the CNN Weather app

London, along with other parts of southeast England, is at the epicenter of a subsidence problem, which is being fueled by unusually hot and dry weather. As heat waves dry out the city's soil, the ground is shifting and shrinking, pulling buildings down with it.

"Subsidence is one of the most damaging geohazards in the UK today," said a spokesperson for the British Geological Survey, or BGS. And experts warn the problem is only going to worsen as humans continue to burn fossil fuels and heat the planet.

London, like many parts of the UK, is built on clay. When wet, it acts like a sponge, sucking up moisture and expanding; in hot and dry conditions, it loses water and contracts. It's a process called "shrink-swell," and when the shrink occurs unevenly under the foundations of a building, it can lead to subsidence.

The city is particularly at risk because the specific kinds of clay soils on which it sits contain expansive minerals that are highly susceptible to changes in moisture. It's also typically exposed to some of the country's hottest temperatures.

An important factor is trees and plants. When it gets hot, their roots drive deeper and further in search of moisture to suck from the soil, often seeking out the damper ground beneath nearby homes — drying it out and causing it to shrink.

Older properties tend to be more vulnerable to subsidence, often due to shallower foundations — and more than half of London's homes were built before 1945.

Across many parts of the city, 100% of properties are projected to face possible or probable subsidence risk in 2030, according to data from the British insurance company Aviva. This includes central areas such as Kensington, the City of London and Westminster.

But it's a problem that goes much wider than the capital. When subsidence expert Bob Gibson started in the business 40 years ago, the issue was mostly in London and the south-east of England. "But with climate change it is now affecting many other parts of the UK as well," said Gibson, who is the director of Building & Structural Consultants.

Whenever there is a hot dry summer, there is a "surge" of subsidence claims, Gibson said. In 2025, when the UK endured an extraordinarily hot summer, the insurance industry paid out a record $415 million in subsidence-related claims, up 10% compared to 2024, according to data from the Association of British Insurers, or ABI.

The record may soon be broken. "This year is shaping up to be the biggest ever, as it is the second of two consecutive drought summers with multiple heatwaves," Gibson said.

Insurers paid out more than $97 million for UK subsidence-related claims in the second quarter of 2026, and the average claim reached a record $27,000, more than $2,700 higher than the same period last year, according to the ABI.

"Following the extremely hot and dry weather we saw over July and August this year, it's likely we'll see more subsidence claims over the coming months," said Louise Clark, general insurance policy manager at the ABI.

An Aviva spokesperson said the company had already seen an increase in claims this year and it will likely continue "unless there is significant rainfall."

Subsidence is sometimes subtle and slow moving, but it can be hugely damaging and challenging to address.

There are two ingredients to consider in subsidence risk, said Brunella Balzano, senior lecturer in structural design at Cardiff University in Wales. The vulnerability of the building and the hazard itself. In the case of heat-driven subsidence, there's nothing engineers alone can do to address the hazard. "We cannot remove climate change," Balzano said.

So, they focus on the building. Interventions can include removing trees and vegetation or constructing barriers to isolate their roots from the house's foundations and, at the more extreme and expensive end, underpinning the house by pumping concrete beneath the foundations.

As temperatures continue to rise, and subsidence claims spike, some experts fear insurers may no longer wish to take on the risk. "I think it's possible … that in the near future, subsidence might not be insured anymore," Balzano said.

In London alone, more than 26% of properties could be affected by 2070 if global warming continues at roughly the current pace, according to BGS data.

People are already struggling to secure insurance in high risk areas, Gibson said. "Insurers are jacking-up premiums hugely, or not inviting renewal of subsidence cover," he said. This can make people fearful of reporting cracks to their insurers, which could lead to them invalidating their insurance, he added.

Subsidence is rarely a life or death issue. "It sits on the borderline, in between what's really dangerous and what can be neglected for a while," Balzano said. It's nowhere near as dramatic as homes falling into the ocean, being ripped off their foundations by floods, or burned to the ground in a wildfire.

But it's also not just an irritant. Subsidence can cause major damage, devalue homes, make them hard to sell and cost eye-watering amounts to fix. It's one more part of the general underlying hum of anxiety-fueling challenges climate change is bringing to people's lives.

"We've had setbacks and each season I've been here we've had periods where it's not been going well and from the outside the team can look a little lost.

"And then we've rediscovered what we're all about as a side.

"We've got to find a way back and give ourselves a chance. We need to show more character and resilience."

fullText:
Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk

Taxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged.

The first robotaxis on London’s streets only started this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade.

The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion.

Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth.

Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”.

About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.

While the report acknowledges potential benefits in safety and different skilled jobs in the sector, it said ministers should act early to mitigate the effects on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers, (121,000 in London), as “self-driving vehicles will eventually make much of this work obsolete”.

It notes that almost half of the mileage covered by Waymo’s robotaxis in California occurs with no passenger on board, that the costs of an empty vehicle are minimal without a driver to pay – and that driving around is potentially cheaper than parking.

According to the Department for Transport forecasts, highly automated driving will bring a 24% rise in road miles by 2050, with significant effects on congestion and road speeds.

Taxes should be implemented now before AVs become commonplace, the report urges. It states: “There is not yet a substantial constituency of AV owners who will resist a charge; once there is, taxing them becomes far harder.”

The thinktank calculates that by 2050, an AV charge set to match the social cost of congestion – about 88p per mile – would raise £47bn per year.

David Lawrence, one of the authors of the report, said that the experience of fuel duty, introduced in 1909 before mass car adoption, showed it was best to build up before “a political fight later on – our view is that now is the time to do it”.

He added: “In terms of the way that bond markets behave, even if tax revenue doesn’t peak until 2050, that’s still going to affect your 30-year bond yields today, which obviously is something the government is having to deal with. It can have an immediate impact on fiscal headroom, even if the actual revenue doesn’t come until much further down the line.”

Ministers have backed the introduction of AVs as a “transformative opportunity” for UK, heralding the start of robotaxi services in London this year as bringing “cutting-edge technology to British roads, creating thousands of jobs and unlocking billions for the economy by 2035”.

Uber, partnering with Wayve, has started limited AV services in the capital, with Google’s Waymo and the Chinese firm Baidu vying to join. Robotaxis already operate in the US, China and the UAE, and Europe’s first fully driverless taxi trials started in Zagreb, Croatia, this week.

Sarah Gates, VP global affairs and assurance at Wayve, said AVs were “a major growth opportunity for the UK – an industry in which we hold a genuine competitive advantage” and would bring high-value jobs and corporation tax revenues from a share of a £700bn global market.

She added: “A sector-specific tax at this early stage would undermine the government’s growth agenda and send precisely the wrong signal: that the UK will penalise its most promising innovators, rather than give them the conditions to scale and succeed.”

The GMB union, which represents taxi and private hire drivers, said a tax on AVs would not go far enough. Simon Rush, president of the GMB London region drivers branch, said: “Driverless cars threaten the livelihoods of private hire drivers and the businesses that depend on them. GMB has asked the government, TfL (Transport for London), and operators for a plan to reskill and redeploy drivers, but to date our questions have gone unanswered.

“An AV charge could go some way to mitigating the economic disruption caused by the rollout of these vehicles, but we need more.”

fullText:
Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday.

Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras.

OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July.

OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.

But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment.

OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks.

The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.)

OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks.

As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market.

Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal

New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school

Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’

Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI

Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images

The US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation.

Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month.

Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram.

Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners.

In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat.

London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.

Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history.

In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun.

title: London amateur goalkeeper could be next in line for Ugandan throne
description: A goalkeeper from an amateur team in South East London could become king of a Ugandan region after the death of his cousin.
fullText:
An amateur goalkeeper, a vacant throne in a kingdom of Uganda and the search for a new king.

Is this likely to be the most remarkable story of the season?

South East Dons - founded in 2014 by British rapper Andrew 'Don Strapzy' McHugh - are arguably one of the most well-known amateur football clubs in the UK.

And given the situation surrounding their current captain and goalkeeper - George Desmond Kamurasi - that's unlikely to change anytime soon.

The BBC understands the SE Dons player is currently in Uganda to attend the funeral of King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, which is expected to take place before the weekend.

As is tradition, his successor will be named before the burial - and it has been widely reported Kamurasi has been chosen as the region's new king.

Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, but it has several traditional kingdoms that continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

The Tooro Kingdom in western Uganda was ruled by King Oyo from 1995. He died in the United States last week, aged 34, after receiving treatment for an aggressive form of cancer.

Kamurasi, 36, is a direct descendant of the clan of 'Babiito' and cousin to the late King Oyo.

It's a far cry from Bexleyheath in south east London, where Kamurasi has been a key member of the SE Dons team's quest to climb the footballing ladder.

The club recently garnered attention by reaching the second qualifying round of the FA Cup. They are due to play Chichester City on Saturday, 19 September.

Although Kamurasi is yet to comment on the reports, he took to social media to plead for patience and space in relation to the situation.

Writing on X, external he said: "I appeal to all Ugandans to remain patient and allow the Omusuuga and the committee to perform their duties in accordance with our cultural traditions for enthroning a new Omukama.

"Let us focus entirely on mourning my cousin, His Majesty King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV."

King Oyo was the world's youngest serving monarch, having ascended the throne at the age of three.

The vacant throne for the Tooro Kingdom of Uganda has courted much intrigue and speculation.

The Royal Select Committee, which is tasked with confirming a new king, must first create a shortlist that not only includes lineage through bloodlines but also relatives of the deceased monarch.

As is tradition, King Oyo's casket will be escorted to the royal burial grounds with his successor and a few close relatives.

The ceremony will also see the new king throw nine coffee beans into the ground where King Oyo is buried.

Before heading to the palace, where he will have a special meal cooked by someone selected specially to prepare it, he is also expected to 'battle' with someone for the throne.

In the past, all rulers of the region have lived in the area - and in the history of the Tooro Kingdom no-one has ever refused to take the throne.

Although, if that were to be the case, the Royal Select Committee would gather again to choose the next suitable candidate until a successor accepts.
